paragraphs.text: LIVES OF THE NEW EMPERORS. [P. 499] 1. In the year [?] of the world, and the year 81[?] of the Incarnation, Leo the Armenian, the patrician, who later showed himself an apostate, became emperor and reigned for seven years and [?] five months. He was crowned by the patriarch Nikephoros. Two years later he defected to impiety and set aside the written pledge he had made concerning orthodoxy, and so he ran aground like Saul. Saul too reigned lawfully for two years. Then he turned aside, was stripped of divine grace and handed over to an evil spirit, took up arms against his benefactor David, and committed the murder of the priests. [P. 500] In the same way this wretched, God-opposing man, after two years, raged and ran mad against piety and exiled the divine Nikephoros who had crowned him. 2. In his place he ordained a so-called patriarch, Theodotos, a senseless man, or rather a slave, more voiceless than the fish and knowing nothing beyond impiety. From then on he fanned the flames of a merciless persecution against the Church. If, then, one ought to marvel at one bad man changing places with another, one ought to marvel at this man and those around him even more than at the Galatians, who were so quickly turning away from him who called them in the grace of Christ to another gospel, which is nothing other than provoking God to anger and drawing down the divine wrath. For the new Sennacherib, Krum, was elated by his earlier victory [?]. He left his own brother to besiege Adrianople, and six days after Leo's accession he came against the City and went around the walls from Blachernae to the Golden Gate, dis-

-playing the force he had with him. In the meadow by the Golden Gate he performed foul sacrifices. Then he demanded that the emperor make peace on condition that he might fix his spear in the Golden Gate. When the emperor refused, he went back to his own tent, greatly impressed by the walls of the City and by the emperor's well-ordered battle line. So he turned to negotiating a peace agreement and made proposals to test the emperor. 4. The emperor seized the opportunity and tried to have him speared. But he was prevented from carrying it through by the incompetence of the men who did it for him: they wounded Krum but did not strike a mortal blow. Maddened by this, the fiend sent [?] to St Mamas and burned the palace there. He loaded onto wagons the bronze lion of the hippodrome, together with the bear and the dragon of the fountain and the finest marbles, and went back. He besieged Adrianople and took it. Then he crossed over with a great multitude of people, including the noble Macedonians, and encamped on the river Danube. Leo, meanwhile, was carrying out the works of impiety in the [?]

5. [?] A comet appeared in the shape of two bright moons. They joined together and separated again into various shapes, and even took the form of a headless man. This foretold the headless head of those who later rose in revolt against the Christians. These rebels had the vain Thomas as their head and as the leader of their division from the other Christians. [P. 501] Moreover, fearful earthquakes followed one after another, along with famines, droughts and scorching heat in the air, and civil strife broke out in every city and land. These things began from the days of the God-hated [?] fiend, and the horror of civil calamity went on prevailing for a long time. 6. Leo then imitated the founder of this abominable heresy, his namesake and a man of the same character, and set about the heresy. Then he looked for allies and fellow initiates, and found John who was called the Grammarian, or rather a second Jannes or Simon. This man was notorious for divination with bowls, for sorcery and for obscene practices [?]. He also found certain others of like mind, followers of Jannes, Jambres and Simon. He kept these men with him in the palace. Then he summoned Nikephoros, the patriarch of blessed memory, together with the leading bishops and priests who were with him, before the senate, and said: "You know very well that some have arisen who say that icons should not be venerated. If you wish, let them be present and debate about this, and the truth will appear more plainly." 7. The divine Nikephoros gave him no answer.

Instead he said to the magnates standing by: "Tell me, can something that does not exist fall?" They answered, with the firmness of faith, that it cannot. The patriarch asked again: "Did the holy icons fall under Leo and Constantine the Isaurians?" They nodded and said yes. "Then they were certainly standing, and had stood upright from of old. For something that does not exist cannot fall in any way." 8. Then the other bishops put forward similar arguments to overturn the heresy, and the holy bishop of Sardis, Euthymios, spoke out boldly: "Pay attention, O emperor, to what I am about to say briefly. Eight hundred years have passed from the time Christ came upon the earth until now, and everywhere Christ is depicted and venerated in images. What presumptuous man, then, would dare to set aside or unsettle the apostolic and patristic tradition of so long a time? This is especially so since the Apostle says: 'So then, brothers, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions which you received, whether by word [P. 502] or by letter. Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema.'" 9. After him Theodore also answered, the zealous and fervent champion of orthodoxy, the abbot of the Stoudios monastery. He said: "Do not unsettle the order of the Church, O emperor. For the Apostle said: 'And God has appointed some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third shepherds and teachers.' He did not say emperors. The civil order and the army have been entrusted to you. Take care of these, and leave the Church to shepherds and teachers, as the divine word says. But if you will not heed this and stand with our faith, then even if an angel from heaven should wish to turn us aside, we will not listen to him, still less to an emperor." 10. When the tyrant heard this, he boiled over with rage, and the ape roared like a lion. He drove them all out with insults. He banished Nikephoros the Great from the City, likewise exiled Theodore of the Stoudios, and ordained in his place the one from [?] [References: 2 Thess. 2:15; Gal. 1:8 [?]; Eph. 4:11 [?]. …a man. I do not know whether one should call him a man rather than a beast, and one wilder and more bitter than the beasts. What could be more pitiable than this calamity, or more wretched than this misfortune? What an evil came rioting into the imperial power! He was of mixed race and half-barbarian, many-shaped in his ways, base-minded and unstable in his opinions. 11. His immediate origin was well known, for he came from the land of the Armenians, which explains his perverse and malicious nature. But his remote and ancient origin did not spring cleanly from anywhere [?]. So some of the elders relate who know what has long been handed down about him and his forefathers: a most evil offshoot emerged from the race of the Assyrians, from whom his father's blood was said to come. For he was descended from the sons of Sennacherib, [P. 503] who once ruled the Assyrians and received his mortal blow from his own offspring. They raised murderous right hands against their father and stained themselves with a parent's blood. Having slain their father with their own hands, they at once fled as fugitives to the lands of the Armenians and found safety there. From this parricidal seed, bitterly preserved, a murderous fruit sprouted in our own generation. I do not know why this horror was allotted to the Romans as their condemnation. Brought forth into this light by judgments known to Him who permitted it, he was nurtured and grew up in wicked and destructive habits and deeds [?]. 12. So from the Assyrian lioness and the Armenian leopard there sprang, from a bastard and counterfeit begetting, a hybrid, composite and monstrous kind of tiger, uglier than any Armenian or Assyrian. He was Leo, "Lion", in name. He possessed the lion's rapacity in full, but would have nothing to do with its nobility. He was a chameleon: as in his appearance, so too in the many shapes of his soul, because of the treacherous and hidden character of his race. From this came the hidden and unspeakable perversity and guile on which he prided himself. For he contrived to conceal the dark, shifty depths of his mind, which was always inclined to do harm. Somehow he had trained and schooled himself never to let his heart agree with his lips, so that he pondered one thing in his mind and spoke another with his mouth. But his life ran aground on such hatred of good and such wickedness that even his demonic

mind and wickedness, though very hard to detect and grasp, became plain to everyone. When, by God's permission, he took hold of the imperial power, or rather the tyranny, he poured out all his rage and guile against the blameless faith and rivalled in everything the impious Copronymus who had reigned before him. Like him, he entrusted the whole of his life to certain foul and utterly wicked men. They were licentious and [?] for the shamefulness of their lives, corrupted in soul and body, sorcerers, poisoners and deceivers of the people, practised in every kind of vice, and, in a word, men who had denied the godliness of the Christians. 13. These men he gladly welcomed into his household and embraced. He bowed to their vain and soul-destroying teachings and initiations and was enslaved like a slave of sin. The deluded man was lured by the hook of deceit and lawlessness and terribly impaled on it. For they set before him three things to be promised: [P. 504] denial of our exact and orthodox faith, destruction of the divine icons, and persecution of the pious. "In this way," they said, "you will reach the height of prosperity, and will complete the present life for a longer time than anyone else." 14. The vain-minded and brutish man was deceived by these and similar ruinous deceptions. He was already ugly, hard to approach and quite shameful in appearance: his name was a lion's, but what one saw was an ape's. Now he became baser in manner, more arrogant in character and more savage in mind. He was untamed in his impulses, unrestrained and irresistible, more irrational, more oppressive and more tyrannical. 15. For the wretched and miserable man was buoyed up by the false prophecy and the plotting of those sinners, and so he quickly launched the war. First he moved his God-fighting tongue against our sacred doctrines. Then here too he emulated the most impious Copronymus Konon. Like him, he gathered a wicked assembly of charlatans, or rather a Jewish Sanhedrin, and the accursed man became both a member and the president of it. Once again the abomination of desolation is seen in the temple of the Lord, and a mouth is opened speaking great things against the glory of the Lord, boasting and vaunting itself against the divine dispensation. And so the second Caiaphas, with that Christ-fighting band, poured out many vain and empty words against the truth. Then he tore down every sacred image set up in the Church, out of hatred for Christ and for his servants. For Christ was a burden to him, whether seen in an image or brought to mind, and so were Christ's friends and servants.

…that the setting up of images is rejected by divine Scripture and quite unknown to it. What, then, might one say to this? O the unsearchable words of the wisdom of God! And the fool will speak folly. Being exceedingly ignorant and silly, he certainly did not know of those golden Cherubim which the sacred initiator Moses fashioned at God's command, and which the old tabernacle of the Law bore above the ark. These were glorified not only among the Jews: the herald of grace also plainly calls them "Cherubim of glory", that is, glorified ones. [P. 505] Then there is everything that Solomon built in his wisdom, and what was seen by the inspired Ezekiel, and whatever else of the kind is recorded and honored in the sacred books. The wretched, profane man did not shudder to place all these among the idols, choosing to reject the God-inspired Scriptures rather than accept them. For this reason he and those of like mind might fairly be thought even more faithless and unreasonable than the Jews. Truly they thought and proclaimed things worthy of their own loathsomeness, unbelief and irrationality. 17. For here too they openly fight against Christ. He took a bright linen cloth, impressed on it his divine likeness, surpassingly bright and beautiful, and sent it in good faith to Abgar, ruler of the Edessenes, who had asked for it. From that time until today, following apostolic tradition and instruction, we reverently depict and venerate these things, so that we may know and remember what Christ did and suffered for us, as is recorded in the sacred books of the Gospels. And we do so even if the Christ-fighters burst with rage. 18. Besides these, a tradition and an account that carries conviction has come down to us: that the divine evangelist Luke painted our Lord Jesus Christ in an image, and also his all-immaculate Mother, and that the city of the Romans preserves these sacred depictions. And what need is there to speak of the other images in Jerusalem? Some who saw them with their own eyes have recorded that very many sacred pictures, set up with care long ago, are still faithfully and piously honored with reverence and venerated there to this day. Again, it is likewise recorded that Peter and Paul, the chief of the apostles, while preaching the mighty works of God in Rome and the miracles Christ had performed, first depicted the divine Transfiguration and handed it down to the Romans: Christ as he appeared to Moses and Elijah, in the midst of the holy prophets. This too is preserved to this day.

19. How, then, do these impious and senseless men answer the miracle in the church of the Mother of God in the city called Lydda, which is celebrated in song and seen to this day? The apostles built that church while she was still alive in this life. [P. 506] For many have seen the venerable image there, not made by hands, reverently venerated and honored. It is imprinted on bright, translucent slabs and goes right through their whole depth. Some of the hostile pagans and Jews tried hard to scrape it off, but they labored in vain and failed in their outrageous attempt. For the more they scraped at the imprint, the more brightly it shone. The figure stands no less in its form, and its appearance, its robe and everything else one sees remain indelible and unharmed. For it is recorded that the holy apostles, at the promise of the all-pure Theotokos, raised a church in her name. At their request she went in to see the church, and stood by one of the columns, and her imprint was found on that column. As has been said, pagans and Jews, despite much violence, could not scrape it off. 20. That the making and tradition of these images is very ancient is witnessed, among other things, by the divine statue which the woman with the issue of blood set up to Christ her healer beside her own house. It was a most vivid monument and an unimpeachable herald of the miracle done for her, proclaiming to later generations the marvel worked on her behalf. Eusebius, the great teacher of the image-makers [?], mentions it in his Ecclesiastical History. He tells of the miracles performed by the sacred, God-grown plant that sprang up there, and how it was a remedy against every ill for all. Then he adds: "We have also learned that images of the apostles Peter and Paul, and of Christ himself, have been preserved in colors in paintings." 21. Sight also bears witness, an unerring teacher. The length of time clearly shows it, as does the building of the venerable churches. So too does the making and dedication of sacred vessels by the pious from long ago, which are countless in number. More than that, there are the very covers of the holy Gospels, which bear the sacred figures on the outside and are reverently venerated by all the faithful. There are also the divine columns, and the so-called soleas that wall off the holy sanctuary of the altar. For for no

other reason [P. 507] than that they should be venerated were these figures piously depicted there from the beginning, together with the figure of the cross set beside them. 22. But the man with a beast's name and a lion's manners set all this aside. He was eager above all to drive out every divine icon and consign it to deep oblivion. So, fighting against God and daring such things before the people, the thunderstruck man spoke boldly, saying: "Brothers, just as we have destroyed the icons before your eyes, so you too, as servants and friends of God and of the emperor, must strive to remove them from your souls." For the fool will speak folly, and his heart will devise vain things, to work lawlessness and to speak error against the Lord. From then on, the bloodthirsty fiend condemned to terrible punishments and chastisements anyone found possessing an icon of Christ or of any saint and venerating it. In this way the godly were cut up like meat every day and slaughtered, and they perished everywhere. He also murdered many illustrious and distinguished men. 23. These things he did against the orthodox without sparing and without ceasing. But against those in office and the wealthier, the wicked and endlessly scheming man devised another wicked plan. He wanted to make them pitiable and poor, so what does he do? He entangled them in charges and accusations they could not escape, making excuses for sins, so that out of fear of the charges they would spend all their property to save themselves. Sometimes he also used force against those who were braver or more gifted. He envied them their courage or their talents and suspected they would rebel. Some he blinded, and others he mutilated. Others he kept in chains and after some days sent to their deaths. Among these was Michael, who held the command of the Excubitors. He had been accused to the emperor of plotting against him, and the emperor kept him under guard in prison and in irons. 24. When the day of our Saviour's Nativity came, the emperor wanted to kill him by night. But his own wife held him back because of the feast, and he let Michael be. Michael, in prison, learned of this and sent word to all his fellow conspirators: "Unless you hurry to get me out of custody, I will denounce all of us to the emperor." Now there were with [?]

…among them was also the papias of the palace, who was a kinsman of Michael. At night these men armed themselves, carrying their swords hidden beneath their clothes, and when the papias opened the gates they came in dressed as priests in phelonia. When the emperor entered the church, they leapt upon him and [?] his unholy soul … in the palace, where none of those who had reigned before him had ever been killed. 25. At that very hour they went to the prison, brought Michael out and led him into the feast, now wearing a crown instead of chains, so that the Psalmist's saying was fulfilled in them: "Weeping shall lodge in the evening, but joy comes in the morning." After this they wrapped the wicked man's limbs in cheap rags, threw his utterly foul body into a small boat, carried it to the island called Prote and buried it there. There they also tonsured his sons and made them monks. I do not know why they were condemned to receive this misfortune in return for so many evils.

26. It should be noted that if the argument of these impious and ill-named men had any strength, and if what they fabricated had any appearance of truth, it would surely have been preserved and known somewhere in the other patriarchates as well. As it is, no trace of it can be found anywhere. For East and West alike continue to uphold this evangelical and apostolic preaching. Under no other authority where there are Christians is that lawless, illicit, God-hated dogma found, which sprang up alien to the piety of Christians. Its wicked and abominable writings have not even come to mind there. It is found only in this enslaved and captive realm, which uses its power to make sport of divine things, and where the earthly, irrational and arrogant mind of those who turn about the earth and wriggle in it, given over to passion and matter, holds sway. There reign self-love, love of power, love of pleasure and love of glory, the enjoyment of every desire, the wish to rule over all and not to be ruled even by God himself, and the acquiring and hoarding of human glory, or rather, shame. Hence too the insolence against

God and the saints, and the persecution of the Church. Hence the subjects, dominated or tyrannized, are forced to bow to their dogmas and wishes. For this purpose the living weapon was forged and improvised: in appearance it was gathered to guard the emperor's person, but in truth it was devised to sack and plunder the Church of Christ. Their pretext, as they rave, is that the divinity of Christ is circumscribed along with him in the icon. It is as if someone were to show this disk-shaped body of the sun painted somewhere, as can be seen in some places, and they then decreed that the substance and radiance of its light were also depicted and circumscribed, or else that the light was entirely cut off from the sun. Or again, as if someone saw a sun's ray falling on a tree, and the tree were then cut down, and it were senselessly supposed that the ray was cut down with it. They will reason the same way about fire and other things, so that they will justly be mocked by children at play, since their thinking is more foolish than theirs. For if in the cases mentioned this cannot by nature happen or be seen, and there is not even room to say it, how much more impossible and unthinkable is it to say or think such things of the ineffable and divine nature, or of the inexpressible and inexplicable dispensation of Christ! For neither when he took flesh nor when he suffered for us in the body did he undergo this. Otherwise, if a man like us were depicted in his body, his soul would necessarily be depicted with it, or else he would certainly be dead, the two being separated; for what else is death but the separation of soul and body? So in these matters they plainly show themselves no less impious than ignorant. They do not know how much difference and distinction there is between the depictable and the circumscribable, between depicting and circumscribing, and so, deceived, they talk nonsense. Where in all the ages has anyone ever heard of a body that cannot be depicted or circumscribed? Or how will the definition and principle of a body be preserved unless it has these properties? So whoever does not hold that Christ is depicted or circumscribed in his body either does not know what a body is, and therefore has no right belief, or else knows it and refuses to admit that body and soul are preserved. Whoever confesses that Christ took on a body like ours, and that ours is depictable and circumscribable, must necessarily also confess that the body of Christ is depictable and circumscribable. If he will not grant the second, then neither will he grant the first, which is wholly absurd and ridiculous. We, then, do not circumscribe; we depict. And the wretches babble yet another, still more absurd thing. The one they call uncircumscribable they somehow, in their simplicity, fantastically claim is circumscribed along with the icon. I do not know how.

But if they babble again that Christ must not be depicted at all, then the Charybdis of their teachers, Mani, Valentinus and Marcion, gapes wide for them. For if they hold that the divine Word took flesh only in seeming and appearance, they will be impaled on a blasphemy no less than their earlier lie, since they impiously set themselves against the whole dispensation and do not blush. And who are these people? The accusers of those who are praised, those who are in darkness about the light, the uneducated in matters of wisdom, the ungrateful creatures, in the words of the Theologian.

THE REIGN OF MICHAEL THE STAMMERER. 1. In the year [?] from the creation of the world, and 8[?] from the incarnate dispensation, Michael the Stammerer, of Amorium, became emperor. He reigned 8 years and 9 months and died of strangury and a most violent pain of the kidneys. He relaxed the prevailing wickedness a little, enough that those in prisons, hardships and exile could imagine a dreamlike freedom and relief. Yet he fostered the God-hated mind of his ill-named and impious predecessor, and likewise was caught on the same hook of the terrible heresy out of utter irrationality and lack of education. So at a silentium he said: "Those before us who examined the exact meaning of the doctrines will be called to account for them, whether they decreed well or badly. We choose to remain in the path in which we found the Church walking." 2. He had a son by Euphrosyne named Theophilus, whom he crowned in the Great Church. He decreed that no one should be free to raise any discussion about icons. Instead, he said, let the synod of Constantine, the synod of Tarasius and the one held now under Leo concerning such questions all be set aside and done away with, and let deep silence fall over the memory of icons. 3. In his reign Thomas the rebel, having already set out from the eastern regions and gathered and dragged along with him a vagabond and mixed rabble, moved against Byzantium, aiming at an empire beyond his station. He came from the land of the Romans, a man of low birth and obscure, and went to the regions of Syria, where he renamed himself Constantine and claimed to be the son of the Empress Irene. And from there

he deceived many barbarians and Christians, gathered a countless host from various nations, and came against Constantinople with a heavy crowd and a great fleet. He had assembled the many kinds of peoples like some [?] beast, multiform, many-colored and many-headed, and like another Sennacherib armed against the new Jerusalem, he boasted and swaggered over the multitude of his followers. He seems not to have realized at all that "A king is not saved by great power, and a giant will not be saved by the greatness of his strength," that "a horse is a false hope for safety," and that "the Lord scatters the counsels of nations," and the rest. For even though the city certainly did not have a Hezekiah, I mean a pious and virtuous emperor, the Lord of all, the lover of mankind, did not overlook his city and his people under siege. Because of the misery of the poor and the groaning of the needy he said then too, "Now I will arise," and "I will defend my city and my people"—not "for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant," as he said then, but now he says, "for my own sake and for the sake of my Son, sprung from the seed of David, and for the sake of the new Jerusalem, which I have chosen"

4. So too in the days of the impious Ahab, when the Syrian had gathered many myriads against him, swaggering and saying, "If the dust of Samaria will suffice for all my people, for my foot soldiers," the compassionate God at once easily removed the reproach from the thrice-wretched king, saying, "Behold, I am giving him into your hands, and you shall know that I am the Lord." And so it happened. At once he showed both his own people and outsiders his own might, and showed that David spoke the truth: "The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle." For when battle was joined, Israel struck down twelve myriads of the enemy. And so that both sides might learn that the blow came from God, the wall of a certain city fell on those who had escaped and buried twenty-seven thousand of them. 5. The vain-minded Thomas adopted this same arrogance of the Syrian and the Assyrian and laid siege to Constantinople, or rather the City of God, for a whole year, while the citizens bravely stood against him, fighting from the walls and at sea.

Because of the sins of the people and the impiety of the rulers, these now for the first time began to humble the affairs of the Christians and bring them under their hand

10. While matters stood thus, Michael departed this life miserably from strangury and pain of the kidneys, and his son Theophilus succeeded to the rule in his place, together with his mother Euphrosyne.

THE REIGN OF THEOPHILUS. In the year 6326 from the creation of the world, and 829 [?] from the divine incarnation, Theophilus became emperor and reigned 12 years: the new Belshazzar, a transgressor, hated by God, an insulter and destroyer of the holy icons, and profane. His mother Euphrosyne sent out to all the themes and brought in beautiful girls in order to find a bride for her son Theophilus. She brought them all into the palace, to the hall called the Triclinium of the Pearl, and gave Theophilus a golden apple, saying, "Give this to whichever one pleases you." Among them was a girl of noble family named

Icasia, who was very beautiful. Theophilus [?] greatly admired her beauty and said, "So it was through a woman that evil things flowed." She answered with some modesty, "But it was also through a woman that better things sprang forth [?]." Stung to the heart by her words, he passed her by and gave the apple to Theodora, who came from Paphlagonia. He crowns Theodora in the oratory of St Stephen, and he himself was crowned with her by the patriarch Antony, with both the crown of marriage and the crown of empire, on holy Pentecost. From there he went in procession to the Great Church and bestowed generous gifts on the patriarch, the clergy and the senate. Icasia, having failed to win the throne, built a convent. There she took the veil, and by ascetic discipline and the life of philosophy she lived for God alone until the end of her life. She also left a great many compositions: "Lord, the woman fallen into many sins," the tetraode of Holy Saturday, "Senseless old man," and some others. The emperor's mother Euphrosyne left the palace of her own accord and lived in quiet in her own convent, called Gastria. 2. Theophilus held horse races and ordered Leo Chamaidrakon, his protovestiarios, to bring the chandelier that had been cut by a sword when Leo the Armenian was slain. When the races were over, he summoned the whole senate to the place called the Kathisma, brought out the chandelier, showed it to them, and said, "He who enters the temple of the Lord and murders the Lord's anointed, what does he deserve?" The senate answered, "He deserves death, O master." At once he ordered the prefect to seize those who had killed Leo together with his father Michael and to behead them in the Sphendone. They protested loudly and said the judgment was unjust: "For if we had not fought alongside your father, O emperor, you would not be reigning." And so their heads were cut off before the eyes of all. The pretext was that they had dared to commit murder in the temple of the Lord. In truth, it was because they had killed his fellow heretic, who shared his impious views. For the wretch held to that man's God-hated heresy and kept away from true piety. Some icons he pulled down, others he dug out, and he exiled and tortured the monks for their devotion. 3. In his reign the Saracens came with a large force against the homeland and city of the wicked tyrant. They found it strongly fortified and very secure, guarded by fifty generals with their picked men and armies. Yet within 15 days, in the month of August, they sacked it, took it by storm, and carried off as captives

[?]…they [marched out?] and killed countless people. What is more, great numbers of their ships set out, laid waste the Cyclades islands, and took Crete and Sicily. And there was severe cold, a most savage and bitter winter, a hard famine, [?] droughts, foul weather and disorders of the seasons, and fearful earthquakes one after another. All these exposed the boundless wickedness and villainy of the ruler. For the godless man had run aground on such hatred of God and such madness that he took over and revived the grievous and utterly abominable heresy of Copronymus and of those named after beasts. So the deluded, empty-headed man proved no less than they in impiety and drunken violence, in tyranny and stupefaction. Gripped by the same deceit, derangement and frenzy as those impious and murderous men, who had sprung from Manichaean madness and Arian rage, he too once again launched a persecution against the Church in the same way.

4. To this man, whom it is better to call a hater of God than a lover of God, Theophobus the Persian fled together with his father, along with fourteen thousand Persians. The emperor distributed these among the themes, settled them, and organized them into tourmai, which to this day are called the tourmai of the Persians. Theophobus himself he made his brother-in-law, marrying him to a sister of Theodora Augusta.

5. This same Theophilus loved splendour. Through the chief of the goldsmiths, a very learned man and a relative of Patriarch Antony, he had the Pentapyrgion made, and the two great organs of solid gold, which he adorned with various stones and [?]. He also had a golden tree made, on which birds perched and sang musically by means of a mechanism. The emperor also renewed the imperial robes. He refurbished them and had the so-called loroi and all the rest made of gold-woven cloth.

6. He put on a show of worldly justice, though he had wronged the faith and true religion more than the emperors before him. Once at Blachernae (for he was in the habit of going there) a widow came up to him and cried out that she was being wronged by Petronas, the Augusta's brother, who was droungarios of the Watch. "He is raising his own buildings higher with the additions he is putting up," she said, "and he is putting mine in darkness and making them worthless, because I am a widow and despised." At once he sent Eustathius the quaestor, surnamed Monachos, who lived in Ozeia, with Leo Symbatios and De-

metrius Kamoulianos, to see whether the new building was wronging the woman. They went and saw the injustice for themselves, and they confirmed that what the woman had said was true. Then they returned and reported to the emperor. Convicted by them before the emperor's eyes, Petronas was stripped in the middle of the street and beaten hard on the back. The quaestor and the antigrapheis were ordered to go, raze those buildings to their foundations, and hand the site over to the woman.

7. This emperor took Alexius the Armenian, surnamed Mosele, a brave and strong man, as his son-in-law, marrying him to Maria, his beloved daughter. He made him a patrician, and shortly afterwards a magistros. Then, because he had certain suspicions that Alexius coveted the throne, he sent him out as general and duke of Sicily. Envy was at work, and some Sicilians came up to the City and slandered him to the emperor: "He is betraying what belongs to the Christians to the Saracens, and he is plotting against your majesty." Meanwhile Maria, the emperor's beloved daughter, died. He adorned her coffin with silver and issued a charter of immunity for those who took refuge there on any charge. Later the emperor Leo removed this silver from

8. When the slander against Alexius was made, the bishop Theodore, called Krithinos, happened to be in the City. Theophilus summoned him, gave him his own token of safe-conduct, and sent him to Sicily to give Alexius a guarantee of safety and bring him back to the City. Theodore went, and with his natural intelligence he persuaded Alexius and brought him to the emperor. The emperor had him beaten as a rebel and put in prison, and confiscated all his property. . . . [?] . . . he laid on Alexius, saying, "It is through me that you have suffered all these terrible things." Then, when the emperor went to Blachernae as was his custom, the archbishop went ahead of him and stood inside the sanctuary, wearing his priestly vestments. As the emperor approached the solea with the senate, the archbishop called out in a loud voice: "Bend your bow, prosper, and reign, for the sake of what, O emperor?" Out of respect for the senate the emperor answered: "For the sake of truth and meekness and justice." The archbishop said: "And what justice is there in you? Through me you gave Alexius a sworn pledge, and you did not keep it!" Stung by this rebuke, the emperor had him dragged out of the sanctuary by force, had many blows inflicted on him, and sent him into exile. It was not only because the archbishop had rebuked him, but also because he had learned that the man honoured and venerated the holy icons and denounced the emperor's impiety. Not long afterwards the emperor came to the Great Church, and the patriarch reproached him. So he brought the archbishop back and begged his pardon. But the archbishop judged himself unworthy of the priesthood because of what he had suffered, so the emperor
made him oikonomos of the Great Church. He also released Alexius from prison and gave him back all his property, keeping him in

9. There was also Manuel, the most renowned of all the generals in the East, who was held in honour by the emperor. He had exchanged some words with Myron, who was logothete of the drome and father-in-law of Petronas. At Myron's prompting Manuel was slandered to the emperor by Basil [?], who claimed he coveted the throne, and terrible things were being planned against him. But Leo the protovestiarios stood up for Manuel, looked after his interests, and assured the emperor that what was said against him was false. Manuel learned of this. To escape the emperor's anger and the slanders, he slipped out of the City in secret and went as far as Pylai. There he mounted the horses of the public post and fled all the way to the mountain passes of Syria, hamstringing the horses behind him. He sent this message to the Hagarenes: "I am fleeing the emperor's anger. If you will not force me to give up my faith, I will take refuge with you. If you will receive me on these terms, send me a guarantee of safety." They welcomed this with great joy and sent a guarantee, and they received him as if he were an emperor of the Romans.

10. When the emperor learned of this he was greatly distressed and downcast, and he took counsel about it with John the synkellos. John said: "If you truly want Manuel to come back, O emperor, I am ready to do it myself. I will take money and be sent to the Amermoumnes, as though to visit those held in prison and in chains. I will also carry a signed pledge from your majesty, and with it I will persuade Manuel to come before you. I expect to succeed through your majesty's signed pledge, through my own powers of persuasion, through his piety, and because it is only natural for a man to love his homeland." The emperor gave him a great deal of money and gifts for the Amermoumnes and sent him off.

11. John arrived with much money and every kind of finery, so that even the Hagarenes were astonished at his wealth. He distributed gifts in the prisons and met the protosymboulos. He also managed to speak with Manuel in secret and give him the signed pledge and the emperor's token of safe-conduct. Having done this he returned and reported to the emperor all he had accomplished. Manuel, for his part, asked the Amermoumnes for leave to march out against a nation hostile to them, and his request was granted. He took the son of the Amermoumnes and a very large army, set out, and won a great victory. For this he was raised to greater honour than before, and with the Amermoumnes he became all-powerful [?]

…Romania, after some time he said to the grandees of the Amermoumnes: "If you give me the son of the Amermoumnes and an army, I will march out and subdue Romania." They told the Amermoumnes and sent him off. When he came near the theme of the Anatolikon, he called together his own men and the son of the Amermoumnes, as though to go out riding and hunting. When they were some distance from the enemy, he embraced the son of the Amermoumnes, kissed him and said: "I am going to my emperor and my own people, for I value nothing in life above my homeland and my kin. But you and your men may go back to your own people, fearing no harm from us." So the young man went back, in tears and in shame, while Manuel made his way to the emperor, sending a messenger ahead to announce his coming.

13. The emperor welcomed the messenger as the bearer of great good news and honoured him with money and dignities. He received Manuel as he deserved. At once he made him magistros and domestic of the Schools, and he stood sponsor for his children at holy baptism.

14. Elated by these events, the emperor marched out against the Hagarenes with Manuel, the senate and the whole army. He easily took Zapetra and Samosata, which were then abounding in wealth and strength because the Amermoumnes came from there. He came back exulting in his victory and his spoils. When he reached Bryas, he ordered a palace to be built there, gardens to be planted and water to be brought in, and this was done. From there he came to the City and celebrated a triumph with the spoils. He held horse races and drove in the first race himself, riding a white chariot and dressed in the colour of the Blues. He won and was crowned, while the demes shouted: "Welcome, incomparable champion [?]!"

15. When Patriarch Antony died, John the synkellos was consecrated in his place. He was, so to speak, the new Jannes and Jambres, notorious for sorcery, divination by basins and every kind of impiety. He was found to be a fit instrument for the emperor's impiety and inclinations, and he worked everything toward the emperor's ruin. The emperor, that petty king of impiety [?], had been in labour with his impiety but had held it back. Now he let it burst forth and brought it to birth, ordering the holy icons to be smeared over or erased.

16. This Jannes built a house of hewn stone outside the city, which to this day is called the Troulos. There, through certain sacrifices, he conversed with demons and revealed the future to the emperor. The house remained uninhabited because of the visitations of demons that took place in it at that time.

18. So Theophilus, the second Nectanebo, had as ally and accomplice in his heresy this John, or rather Jannes,

the patriarch, or rather [?]-arch, a truly new Apollonius and Balaam, who appeared to our misfortune in our own times as a diviner by basins and a dreadful expounder of every God-hated practice and trickery. It was by him that the fickle and treacherous emperor had been taught his letters, and so he became a proven servant of the most hateful deeds and a fit instrument of the devil. On such men the divine word would justly pronounce its lament and curse: "Woe to them, for they went the way of Cain, and for the sake of gain they rushed headlong into the error of Balaam, and perished in the rebellion of Korah. These are grumblers and malcontents, following their own desires in their deceptions."

The words with which the Theologian's tongue pilloried Julian, a man of the same character, would also fit him very well. For he proved very like Julian, and in no way different from him in villainy and perversity. Gregory said: "How can I not weep for the wretch? How can I not lament, more than those who were persecuted, those who ran over to him? And more than those who deserted to wickedness, how can I not lament the one who carried them off? Or rather, for the first it is no hardship to suffer for Christ, but the most blessed thing of all. That is so not only because of the world to come, but also because of the glory and boldness here that they won for themselves through their dangers. For the others, what they have already suffered is a prelude to what awaits them. It would have been better for them to be punished here for longer than to be kept back for the just judgments there. They say the chameleon easily takes on every hue and changes into every colour except one, white. In the same way that man was and became everything to Christians except gentle. His humaneness was utterly inhuman, his persuasion was violence, and his kindness was an excuse for savagery."

Therefore one must say to him: "Most foolish of men, utterly ignorant in great matters, did you rise up against so great an inheritance and against the whole world? Did you set yourself against the Church of Christ and its sacrifice with your [?]? Did you set yourself against the blood that cleanses the world with your own foul bloodshed? You are a persecutor after Herod, and a traitor after Judas, except that you did not show your repentance by the noose as he did. You are a Christ-killer after Pilate, a God-hater after the Jews, an insulter of the saints. Would it be more fitting to call you Jeroboam, or Ahab the Israelite, those most lawless men, or Pharaoh the Egyptian, or Nebuchadnezzar the Assyrian? Or shall we put them all together and call you by all their names at once? For you clearly gathered into yourself the vices of all of them:

the apostasy of Jeroboam, the bloodthirstiness of Ahab, the hardness of Pharaoh, the sacrilege of Nebuchadnezzar, and the impiety of all of them together. Where are the sacrifices and rites and mysteries? Where are the victims, seen and unseen? Where are the marvels of foreknowledge and the signs from ventriloquists? Where are the divinations and threats against Christians? All are gone, all proven false, all have melted away. The boasts of the impious have turned out to be a dream. Bel has fallen, Dagon is shattered. Never again will they tell the fool to rule [?]. And perhaps these things now seem small to the wretches. But a time will come when I shall see those who insulted me, and their great leader, bewailing their own wickedness, when all wickedness and evil are judged and punished."

18–19. While these things were being done by the emperor and the patriarch who shared his secret rites, the Arabs marched out with a great force against Romania. The emperor advanced against them with the Persian refugees, the tagmata, and Manuel the domestic. When battle was joined, the emperor was defeated. He went into the midst of the Persians, expecting that they would keep him safe. Looking around, Manuel saw that the emperor was among the Persians. He realized that they meant to betray him to the Arabs and make their peace with them through him. So he cut his way through their midst, seized the bridle of the emperor's horse and drove him out against his will. He thought it an unbearable disgrace for the Romans if the Arabs took the emperor of the Romans captive. But the emperor, beside himself with fear at the situation, wanted to flee back to the Persians. Manuel raised his sword as if to strike him. Then the emperor took fright and followed unwillingly, and so was barely saved. From there he returned to Dorylaeum in shame after a heavy defeat. Manuel had been wounded in the battle. He fell ill and died, having performed many brave deeds against the Hagarenes. His body was carried back and laid in the monastery of Manuel that he himself had founded, near the cistern of Aspar.

At once slanders against the Persians reached the emperor, along with threats against Theophobus as a rebel, a traitor and an enemy. When Theophobus learned of this, he took the Persians, went down as far as Sinope, seized it and held it as a usurper. When the emperor learned this he was greatly troubled, for he feared they might go over to the Arabs. He went in person as far as Paphlagonia and gave them a pledge that they would suffer no harm. Then he took Theophobus and returned with him to the City, while the other Persians went back to where they had first been settled. Theophobus was loved by the citizens as an Orthodox man no less than he was loved by the Persians.

21. Then, as the emperor was going to Bla-

chernae, as was his custom, a man came to meet him and said: "The horse your majesty is riding is mine." The horse shied at the man's sudden approach. The emperor reined it in and asked the count of the stable: "Whose horse is this?" He answered: "The count of the Opsikion sent it to your majesty." The count happened to be in the City, so the next day the emperor brought him in, together with the man who had approached him. He said to the man: "Tell the truth: whose horse is this?" He answered: "It was mine. The general sent men and took it from me by force, and gave me neither payment nor rank." The emperor said to the count: "Tell me whether this is so, and why you sent it to me without first settling the matter of the horse." He answered: "He was asking to be made a scholarios. Since I did not know whether he was brave, I offered him a hundred nomismata, but he would not take them." The emperor said: "Then why did you send me the horse without reaching a full settlement with him?" The emperor looked into the matter and was fully satisfied that the count had taken the horse by force. He punished the general with a fitting flogging and gave the horse back to the man who had approached him. But the man did not want to take it back. Instead he accepted two pounds of gold for it, and the general was ordered to test him and make him a scholarios if he proved brave. Later he went to war, but in the battle he turned out to be a coward. He was found among those fleeing and was cut down by the enemy.

22. While the emperor was on an excursion at Bryas, a message came to him from the general of the Anatolikon that the protosymboulos had set out with a large host and was on his way to sack Amorion. The emperor quickly did what was customary for the army and the officers and set out as far as Cappadocia. The Amermoumnes detached fifty thousand men and sent them against the emperor, putting at their head Soudaes [?], who was most renowned among the Hagarenes for courage and good sense. Battle was joined, and the emperor was defeated. He fled and came back in shame, barely saved. The Amermoumnes went with a great force and besieged Amorion. He launched many assaults but could not take it, for those inside fought nobly and steadfastly. Now there was in the fortress a disciple of Leo the Philosopher. When the Amermoumnes was ready to withdraw, this astronomer sent him word through someone: "If you hold out at the fortress for two more days, you will take us." And so it happened, for the city was betrayed by a man called Boiditzes and by the Manikophagos [?]. Among the notables, men of good birth were captured and taken off to Syria as prisoners: Theophilus the patrician and general, Melissenus, Aetius, Theodore the protospatharios, the eunuch Krateros, and [?]

Callistus the tourmarch, Constantine the droungarios, Basoes the runner, and many others, including officers of the tagmata. The protosymboulos tried to force them to deny their faith. When they would not be persuaded, they were beheaded with the sword, exchanging the present life for the life eternal.

23. But the disciple of Leo the Philosopher exchanged the noblest salvation for a shameful survival. He went over to the Amermoumnes, who asked him about his learning. He said he was a disciple of Leo the Philosopher. When the Amermoumnes learned who Leo was and what sort of man he was, he longed to see him. So he gave a letter for Leo the Philosopher to one of the captives and sent him to Constantinople, promising that if Leo came to him he would be held in honour from then on. Leo received the letter, and fearing it might be discovered, he took it up to the emperor Theophilus. Only then did the emperor learn of Leo's learning and realize that he had so wise a man in his realm. He took him in and kept him in the palace of the Magnaura, entrusting students to him to teach and providing everything he needed. Leo later became metropolitan of Thessalonica.

24. This same emperor built the Trikonchos in the palace, and the so-called Sigma, and the steps where the demes stand. He also set up a fountain, where the so-called [?] takes place, as the horses of both factions pass by with golden [?]. Beneath the Trikonchos, down below, he made by an ingenious device the so-called Mystery: if someone speaks in one corner, he is heard in the other.

25. This same Theophilus learned that Theophanes and his brother Theodore, who lived on their own, were mocking his impiety and exposing it. In his anger he sent for them and had them brought before him, and said: "Where are you from?" They said: "From Palestine." The villain said: "And why, after leaving your own land and coming to ours, do you not obey my majesty?" When they made no answer, he ordered them to be struck in the face [?]. Afterwards he had them flogged with ox-hide whips almost to death. Then in a rage and with a harsh voice he said to the eparch: "Take them to the praetorium and write on their faces, carving these verses:

While all men long to hasten to the city

Where the all-pure feet of God the Word
Stood for the salvation of the world,
These men appeared in that venerable place [?]
[?] of superstitious [?].
There they did many [?] out of perversity,
Shameful and dreadful deeds, with impious minds,
And from there they were driven out as apostates.
But when they fled to the imperial city,
They did not give up their lawless follies.
Therefore, branded on the face as criminals,
They are condemned and driven out once more."

And he added: "Even if the verses are not good, let that not trouble you."

He said this because he knew they were very wise and highly practised in the precise rules of poetic forms, after someone had remarked: "These men are not even worthy of having good iambics." But they said: "Write, emperor, write whatever you please, since this will be read before the just and fearful Christ." The prefect took them to the praetorium, and two days later he stretched them out on benches, bound their hands and feet, pricked and carved the verses into their faces, and sent them into exile. Theodore, who is among the saints, died in exile, while the celebrated Theophanes the poet lived on until the time of Michael and Theodora. He struggled hard for the restoration of Orthodoxy and also became metropolitan of Nicaea, as affairs were already turning toward greater piety...

26. In the reign of Theophilus there was also Joseph the hymnographer, who was exiled by the empress Theodora. His life lasted until the reign of Leo the Wise.

27. In his time the golden plume fell from the statue of Justinian on the column called the Augusteus. Everyone was at a loss, wondering how they might get up to it. Then a craftsman who was a steeplejack was found. He climbed onto the roof tiles of the Great Church and shot an arrow with a rope attached at the bronze horseman of Justinian. When the arrow had lodged there, he ran across along the rope. He amazed the [?] onlookers, fitted the plume back in place, won the emperor's favour and made a great name for both his skill and his natural gifts, and the emperor rewarded him with a hundred nomismata.

28. Theophilus crowned his son Michael in the Great Church and gave generous gifts to everyone at the coronation. He also built a hostel, the one now called "Ta Theophilou." It had been the house of the patrician [?], who came from Rome with [?] in the time of Constantine the Great. Later it was handed over [?] so that noblewomen who did not know how to be chaste lived there. Under Leo the Isaurian, the brothel became a hostel. Afterwards it became the house of Constantine, the son of Irene, after his mother had him blinded. When he died, his wife took the monastic habit, built a monastery there and named it "of Repentance." The house was very large and admirable, but a beam broke off in the dining hall and threatened collapse. The nuns appealed to the emperor about this as he was on his way to Blachernae. He turned aside and looked at the house, and he liked it so much that he moved the nuns to another monastery. He decorated the house with every kind of ornament and turned it into a hostel, assigning to it [?] a very great deal of money,

silver and estates, and he named it "Ta Theophilou."

29. Before his death, this God-hated emperor held a secret council with his like-minded associates about Theophobus the Persian. The Persians under Theophobus and many officials still had great love for him and great loyalty to him, and the emperor said: "When I die, they may plot to seize power against my son, who is an infant, and against my wife." So he brought Theophobus up to the palace and kept him there with him. When his illness grew worse, he imprisoned Theophobus in the vaults of the Boukoleon. The Persians kept asking what had become of him. Then the emperor sent Petronas, the Augusta's brother, by night with the logothete, and they cut off Theophobus's head. These men convinced the Persians that he was with the emperor in the palace. The emperor gave up his soul miserably to dysentery, and his wretched body was carried to the Holy Apostles. They secretly brought Theophobus's body out through the Boukoleon and kept it safe near Ta Narsou, in the place now called "of Theophobia," and they buried it there.

THE REIGN OF MICHAEL WITH HIS MOTHER THEODORA

1. In the year of the world 6339, and from the divine Incarnation 839, Michael the son of Theophilus became emperor. He reigned fifteen years with his mother Theodora, ten years alone, and one year with Basil. He succeeded to his father's throne, and he truly cast off the new God-hated religion that had crept into the Church and run terribly riot there. He proclaimed the holy and most orthodox faith, which had been beloved of God and awarded by God from of old. Theodora was so faithful and orthodox that she secretly honoured and venerated the holy icons even while her husband was still alive. On her own judgment, but also at the suggestion and urging of Theoktistos, the keeper of the imperial inkstand and logothete, she drove the patriarch John and his circle out of the Church and out of the City. She confined him on the Bosporus at the place called Kleidion. It is said that he was also a godparent to her children. She brought in Methodius, now among the saints, who was then a monk, and installed him as patriarch. She reunited all the monks and bishops whom Theophilus had exiled, confirmed the orthodox faith and gave the Church peace on the first Sunday of the holy Fast. 6. This same Theoktistos, who held great influence with the Augusta, built houses, baths and a garden at the place now called Apsis, so that he could be near the palace. 7. A little later, the general of the Boukellarioi brought the emperor a spirited and noble horse. The emperor wanted to harness it for the Hippodrome, so he wished to examine its teeth, which show its age, and to find out what its temperament was like. But the horse grew bold and reared, and the emperor was annoyed, because no one there had enough courage and skill to tame the horse or even just to master it. Seeing his annoyance, Theophilitzes, who was present, said: "Master, I have a young man who is very experienced and [?] with horses, just what your Majesty wants. His name is Basil." The emperor ordered him to come at once. A chamberlain was sent to the Iron Gate, found Basil and quickly brought him to the emperor. When he was ordered to hold the horse, he gripped the bridle with one hand and seized the horse's ear with the other, and he made it as tame as a sheep. The emperor was pleased and delighted, and he handed Basil over to Andrew, who was hetaireiarch, to be enrolled in the Hetaireia and to work with the horses.

8. I have thought it necessary to tell about this Basil: how he was brought up and where he came from, up to this point in the story. Basil was born in Macedonia, in the villages around Adrianople, in the reign of Michael Rangabe. Michael was the father of the patriarch Ignatius and the son-in-law of the emperor Nikephoros through Nikephoros's daughter Prokopia. In Michael's reign Krum, the ruler of Bulgaria, marched out against the Christians. Michael was routed, and Leo the Armenian rebelled against him and became emperor.

He also went to Adrianople, captured it and deported ten thousand men, not counting the women, and settled them beyond the Danube. In the days of the emperor Theophilus there was a general in Macedonia called Kordyles. He had a son named Bardas, a very brave man, whom he left in his place to govern the Macedonians beyond the river Danube. 9. So the people decided to leave for Romania with their wives and children. When Michael the Bulgarian had gone off to Thessalonica, they began to cross with their belongings. When the count learned of this, he crossed over to fight them. In desperation the Macedonians made Tzantzes and Kordyles their leaders. They gave battle, killed many and captured some. Those who could not get back across to Bulgaria fled to the Hungarians and told them all about the Macedonians. The emperor's ships also arrived to take them to the City. The Turks said to them: "Give us all your possessions, and go wherever you like." They refused, and they stayed in battle order for three days. On the fourth day they began to board their ships. The next day, as they were trying to withdraw, the Huns appeared again to fight them. Then a young Macedonian named Leo, of the family of the Gomostai, who later became hetaireiarch, rose up with other notable Macedonians. They routed the Huns and drove them off. So the emperor changed his demeanour and conduct, just as he had changed his heart and mind, and set about grieving her in as many ways as he had before pretended to serve her. He thrust his sisters Thekla, Anastasia and Anna out of the palace and took them down to the Karianos, while Pulcheria, as her mother’s favourite, he sent to the monastery of Gastria. Acclaimed [?] by the senate, he rules alone as autocrat, and promotes Bardas to magistros and domestic of the Scholae. So he removed her too from the palace and sent her as well to the monastery of Gastria. She, unsettled by despondency

in her mind, and robbed of her reason by shock, devised things unworthy of herself: she plotted against Bardas, taking as her accomplice, along with many others, the emperor’s protostrator, intending to kill Bardas as he returned from his suburban estate at Kosmidion. But their scheme was revealed before it was carried out and brought the evil down on those who had planned it: they were detected, seized, and beheaded in the Sphendone. Michael then promotes Basil to protostrator in place of the dead man, and likewise his uncle Bardas to kouropalates. 15. At that time dust fell from the sky onto the roof tiles, full of something like blood, and many people found stones in the streets or gardens as red as blood. Michael promotes Antigonos, Bardas’ son, to domestic of the Scholae. Bardas’ other son, having given him a wife — the very woman over whom Bardas was also slandered — he appointed sole strategos of the West. When this son died soon afterward, Michael promoted his uncle Bardas to Caesar in Easter Week; and Bardas rode in a chariot and distributed the consular largess on the Mese. 16. Amer came out and went down as far as Sinope, plundering all the Roman lands, and returned without being caught by the Roman army. Michael, campaigning together with Bardas the Caesar, moved by land and sea against Michael the ruler of Bulgaria, having learned that the Bulgarian nation was wasting away from famine. When the Bulgarians learned of this they cowered as at a clap of thunder; before any contest or battle they despaired of victory and asked to become Christians and to submit to the emperor and the Romans. Michael baptized their ruler, received him from the font, and gave him his own name; and bringing his magnates into the City he baptized them, and from then on there was deep peace. 17. When Amer had come out against Romania, Petronas, who was general of the East, and Nasar of the Boukellarioi lay in wait for his return and met him at Lalakaon. Battle was joined and they routed Amer; as he fled, one of the counts pursued him, cut off his head, and brought it to Petronas the general. The generals entered the City with victory celebrations and held a triumph for these deeds in the Hippodrome. And from then on there was great peace in the East because of the slaughter of Amer. 18. Yet while the labours and the brave deeds against the enemy belonged to others, the emperor’s love was lavished on Basil, and he alone was to be his favoured attendant. 19. Michael built a stable for his horses, adorning it with marble and making it exceedingly beautiful with running water. When it was finished — there was a certain Peter in the City, a learned and caustic man, whom people called the Ptochomagistros — Michael summoned him to the stable [?] and

showed him the senseless splendour of the building he had made, wanting to be praised by him, and added this: “I shall be remembered forever for building this work.” But he said to the emperor: “Justinian built the Great Church, adorning it with gold and silver and costly marbles, and now there is no remembrance of him. And you, emperor, having made a dung-house and a resting place for brute beasts, say you will be remembered for this?” Disappointed of praise from him and angered, the emperor had the Ptochomagistros thrown out, beaten and dragged. 20. A rumour went about that Bardas the Caesar was carrying on a corrupt affair with his daughter-in-law. When Ignatius the patriarch heard it, he urged him many times to abstain from such defilement and not to be a stumbling block to many, when he ought to be an example of virtue and of a sober life. But he hastened [?] to … [?]. And once, when Bardas was about to receive communion, the patriarch turned him away as one who obeyed neither canons nor admonitions. Struck in his soul with anger, Bardas drove out his admonisher as lawless and a corrupter of the Church, and subjected him to countless savage tortures to make him resign. When he would not give in, Bardas had Photios ordained patriarch in his place, who was then protasekretis and an exceedingly learned man. 21. The emperor went on campaign against the Hagarenes, leaving Ooryphas, who was eparch, in the City to guard it. The emperor turned back from the road he had taken, and accomplished nothing royal or noble in the business for which he had abandoned it. There were two hundred ships, which surrounded the City and struck great fear into those within. The emperor arrived and barely managed to cross over. Then, with hymns, they brought out the holy veil of the Theotokos and dipped its edge into the sea. To Maria, Basil’s former wife, he gave gold and some other things and sent her away to her own home in Macedonia. His own sister Thekla he joined to Basil for him to keep privately. 24. In private Basil slandered the Caesar to the emperor as plotting against him, but the emperor listened to this as nonsense. Basil, eager to convince the emperor, made friends with Symbatios, patrician and logothete of the Drome, who was the Caesar’s son-in-law, and they confirmed with oaths to each other that they would be of one mind and in lasting friendship. The emperor, persuaded by Symbatios’ oaths and confirmed by Basil’s words, swore an oath against the Caesar. Constantine Toxaras … [?] … having saluted him, turned back and informed Basil of the Caesar’s arrival. Basil came out, bowed to him, took him by the hand, and led him to the emperor. The Caesar sat down with the emperor and said: “Since the whole army is assembled, master, give the order for it to cross over to Crete.” Basil, standing behind him, made threatening gestures at the Caesar with his hand. Suddenly the Caesar turned and saw him threatening, and at once Basil struck him with his sword, and the others with him hacked him limb from limb, while the emperor looked on in silence. 29. It was the third hour of the day. The emperor and Basil immediately returned to the City. As they were coming along the road, at the market town of Akritas, where a great crowd had gathered to see the emperor, a man clothed in the monastic habit stood on a high rock and cried out loudly to the emperor: “A fine campaign you have made, emperor, shedding with the sword the blood of your own kinsman and your own [?] blood! Woe to you, woe to you for doing this!” Angered, the emperor

and Basil sent a manglabites … [?] to kill the monk with the sword. But the people ran up to the man who had been sent and pleaded that the monk was out of his mind and possessed by a demon, and so he barely escaped punishment. 30. Late on the Saturday of Pentecost the emperor informed the patriarch Photios, through Rentakios his protovestiarios, that he would proclaim Basil emperor. The next day two thrones were brought out, and the people were troubled that, though there was one emperor, two thrones had been brought out. As the emperor went in procession, Basil walked behind him wearing a skaramangion and a sword, as is the custom for parakoimomenoi. When the emperor entered as far as the imperial gates he did not take off his crown, as is the custom for emperors, but went in wearing it as far as the holy doors. Then, turning around, he went up the steps crowned, with Basil the parakoimomenos below him, and below Basil Leo Castor the asekretis, holding a document in his hands, and [?] Angoures the praipositos, and the demarchs together with the demes. Leo the asekretis began to read, saying: “Bardas the Caesar plotted against me to kill me, and for this purpose he led me out of the City. Had I not been informed by Symbatios and Basil, I would not be among the living. He died through his own sin. It is my will that Basil the parakoimomenos, since he is faithful and guards my reign, has freed me from my enemy and has great affection for me, should be the guardian and steward of my reign and be acclaimed by all as emperor.” Basil was filled with tears. The emperor took the crown from his head and gave it to the patriarch Photios, who carried it to the holy altar and said a prayer over it. The praipositoi brought a divetesion and tzangia and dressed Basil, who put on the chlamys and fell at the emperor’s feet. The patriarch came out, took the crown from the emperor’s head and placed it on Basil. And when the sceptres had been lowered, as is customary, Michael crowned Basil, and all acclaimed: “Many years to Michael and Basil!” Castor the asekretis, who had read out the document, went off to Nicomedia and came to a men’s monastery, where he stayed in the middle of a meadow. There was a well there; he fell into it, drowned, and was buried there. 31. Symbatios, the Caesar’s son-in-law, having failed to gain the rank of Caesar and seeing that he had been made a fool of by Basil, was moved to hatred against him. After taking counsel with George Peganes the general, the next day he asked to be appointed [?]. In his place Goumer was appointed logothete of the Drome, and Peganes count of the Opsikion. Symbatios and Peganes went out together and began to ravage the population and burn

the fields and vineyards (for it was summer), acclaiming Michael alone and repudiating Basil. When the emperors learned this, they ordered the other generals to fight them. Nikephoros Maleinos, after taking counsel, threw a written message among the troops, so that they might take the rebels by stratagem and not fall into civil war by fighting openly. And everyone deserted them. Peganes was captured and brought into the City, and by the emperor’s command Constantine Myares the eparch blinded him; they seated him at the Milion and put a bowl in his hands, and everyone passing by threw him whatever they chose. Thirty days later Symbatios the Armenian was captured by [?] in Keltzene [?]; they blinded him and also cut off his right hand, and seated him at the Lausos with a bowl in his lap, so that anyone who wished might throw him something. After three days they took them back to their own houses, keeping them under guard. 32. The emperor Michael sent a mechanic called Damarios [?] and had Constantine Kaballinos taken out of his tomb; he found the body intact, and when he tried to bring it in in a sack and it would not fit, he wrapped it up. Likewise he took the patriarch John out of his tomb together with his omophorion. By the emperor’s command the eparch shut them up in the praetorium; then on a day of races he brought them out, stripped them, [had them beaten with] whips [?], and took their bones and burned them at the place of Amastrianos. The sarcophagus of Copronymus, which was green and marvellous, he had sawn up and made into panels in the church he had built at the Pharos. 33. The emperor Leo was born of Michael and Eudokia Ingerina while Michael was still alive, on 1 September, in the fifteenth indiction. The emperor also held a race at Saint Mamas, himself driving for the Blues; Constantine the Armenian, father of the patrician Thomas, who was drungarios of the Watch, drove for the Whites; Agalianos drove for the Greens, and Krysas for the Reds. The emperor won, and when he sat down to dinner with Basil and Eudokia, the patrician Basiliskianos praised the emperor for having driven the chariot well. The emperor ordered him to stand up and commanded him to pull off the emperor’s tzangia and put them on himself. When he hesitated and looked toward Basil, the emperor angrily ordered him to do it. Since Basil gave him no sign, he put on the tzangia. And the emperor said to Basil with an oath: “They suit him better than you. For do not [?]

"I have the power [?]: just as I made you emperor, I can make another as well [?]." And he was angry, raging against Basil. Eudokia, weeping, said to the emperor: "The dignity of the imperial office, my lord, is a great thing, and we ourselves were honoured with it beyond our worth; it is not right that it should be held in contempt." The emperor said: "Do not be grieved at this, for I also mean to make Basiliskianos [?] emperor." 35. Basil was full of anger and great grief. When the emperor went out to the hunt, a monk met him and gave him a paper describing the plot that Basil was preparing against him. He read it and, in his anger, began to plan against Basil. When his mother Theodora invited the emperor to the Anthemiou, he sent Rentakios, his protovestiarios, with other men of his household to hunt something and send it to his mother. Basil was making his preparations against Michael and was very sullen. When the emperor sat down to dinner, he invited Eudokia and Basil to dine with him. After the emperor had drunk a great deal of wine, Basil rose as if to relieve himself, went into the emperor's bedchamber and, being a strong man, bent the bolts so that the door could no longer be locked; then he went back and dined with the emperor. When the emperor was drunk once more, with Ingerina rejoicing with him as usual, Michael rose and was led by the hand by Basil into the bedchamber, where Basil kissed his hand and went out. Inside the bedchamber was Basiliskianos [?], sleeping on Rentakios's bed by the emperor's order in order to guard him. Ignatios the chamberlain went to lock the door of the bedchamber, found it bent, and in despair sat down on the bed, tearing his hair. While the emperor, from the wine, slept a sleep like death, Basil suddenly came with others and opened the doors. Ignatios came out in terror and resisted Basil to stop him from entering. Peter the Bulgarian slipped under Basil's arm toward the emperor's bed, but was held back by Ignatios, who resisted him. The emperor woke up. John Chaldos at once struck the emperor with his sword and cut off his hands. Jakobitzes the Persian, the apelates, wounded Basiliskianos with a sword and flung him down headlong. Marianos and Bardas, the father of Basil the rhaiktor, and Symbatios [?], Basil's brother, and Asylaion, Basil's cousin, and Constantine Toxaras stood guard outside, and none of Michael's people knew what was happening. Basil's men gathered together and took counsel. Asylaion said to Basil: "Even though we have cut off his hands, we have left him alive; and if he lives, what defence shall we make?" And to please Basil he went back and found Michael without his hands, lying on the bed and lamenting bitterly against Ba-

-sil. He drew his sword and mercilessly drove it into the emperor's heart, tearing open his entrails. Then he turned and boasted to Basil as though he had performed a great feat of valour. 35. Although there was a storm on the sea, they gathered and went down to the ferry crossing; having crossed, they came to the house of Eulogios the Persian, and taking him with them [?] they came to the quarter of Marina. There was a slab [?] blocking the wall; Basil took hold of two of his companions and, kicking, broke the slab, and they made their way as far as the gate of the palace. Eulogios the Persian spoke in his own language to Artavasdos the hetaireiarch: "Michael has died by the sword; open to the emperor." Artavasdos ran in to the papias, took the keys from him by force, and opened to the emperor. Once inside, Basil took the keys of the palace into his own hands, and the next morning he made Gregory, called the son of Philemon, papias. At once he sent to Saint Mamas and brought Eudokia, the daughter of Inger, into the palace with great pomp. He also sent John the praepositus to take away the Dekapolitissa and bring her back to her own parents. He also sent Paul the chamberlain to bury Michael. Paul went and found him wrapped in the saddle-cloth of the right-hand horse that he used to drive, with his entrails hanging out. There he found his mother and his sisters lamenting and wailing over him; they put him in a small boat and crossed over to the monastery of Chrysopolis, and there they buried him [?].

1. In the year [?] of the world, and [?] of the divine Incarnation, Basil the Macedonian reigned: with Michael one year and four months, and alone [?] years. He ordered the prefect Marianos [?], son of Petronas, to go up to the Forum and, together with all the people, proclaim him sole emperor. 2. I have thought it necessary to record the vengeance that came from God upon those who laid hands on Michael, and what each of them suffered at various times. Jakobitzes, while hunting with the emperor in the Philopation, dropped his sword and dismounted to pick it up; before his foot had reached the ground, the other foot caught in the stirrup, and the horse took fright and dragged him through ravines and [?], tearing him limb from limb. John Chaldos, after becoming general in Chaldia, was caught plotting against the emperor and was impaled by Andrew the general on the emperor's orders. Asylaion, the emperor's cousin, was banished by the emperor himself to his suburban estate called that of the Chartophylax; being harsh and [?] toward his slaves, he was by them, with knives,

[Lives of the More Recent Emperors] slain at night. The emperor seized them, hacked them limb from limb and burned them in the Amastrianon. The Persian's apelates was eaten by worms and departed this life. Constantine Toxaras was cut down with swords among the Kibyrrhaiots and died. And Marianos, the emperor's brother, broke his foot and died eaten by worms. 3. On the day of Christ's Nativity the emperor went out in procession to the Great Church and crowned [?] his son Stephen. Then, bringing white horses with chariots, he took his seat together with the Augusta, and the praepositus Baanes rode with them, carrying the child as far as the palace, while the emperor scattered consular largesse along the way. 4.
