On the feast of Saint Polyeuktos there was a tremendous earthquake, so that the earth shook for forty days. At that time the globe of the statue in the Forum fell, and so did the church of the most holy Theotokos called the Sigma, so that all the chanters there were killed. Leo the Philosopher happened to be there and told the chanters and everyone present to leave the church; but they would not listen, and they all perished. The philosopher himself took his stand by a column under the vaulting [?] and was saved with two others, and five others alone were saved beneath the ambo. 5. When the emperor came into the church and was about to receive communion, the patriarch Photius called him a robber and a murderer and unworthy of the divine communion. Enraged, the emperor sent to Rome and obtained a tome with Roman bishops, drove Photius from the throne, and appointed Ignatius, now among the saints, patriarch for the second time. The emperor Alexander was born of Eudokia, the daughter of Inger; he was Basil's legitimate son. 6. The emperor campaigned against the Hagarenes of Tephrike, joined battle and was defeated; engaging the Hagarenes many times, he lost many of the Romans. During this flight of the emperor, Theophylaktos the Unbearable, father of Romanos who reigned later, saved the emperor when he had very nearly been captured by the Hagarenes. Afterwards the emperor sought him out, found him and recognized him (for many were telling the emperor, "It was I")... and he, declining honours, asked for an imperial estate, which he also received. On returning to the city, the emperor sent his son-in-law Christopher to Tephrike; he won a very great victory, sacked the city and razed it to the ground. 7. The patriarch Ignatius built a very beautiful church at the market of Satyros, in the name of the Archistrategos of the Anatellon [?], and founded a monastery for men there, where his body also lies.

8. When Thekla, the emperor's sister, sent to the emperor, about some memorandum, a man who was her [?], the emperor asked him: "Who is keeping your mistress?" He said: "Neatokometes." The emperor at once sent and brought him, had him beaten, tonsured him and clothed him in the monastic habit. Likewise he sent Prokopios, his protovestiarios, who beat Thekla, took all her money and brought it to the emperor. Afterwards he made Neatokometes steward of the Great Church. 9. This same emperor baptized all the Hebrews who were under his rule at that time, all those holding dignities standing sponsor for them, while the emperor showed kindness to all the Hebrews and gave them assistance and many gifts.

10. As for the Nicholas mentioned earlier, the Andr[?], who was also custodian of the church of Saint Diomedes, and to whom the martyr had appeared concerning the emperor, as was said before: the emperor honoured him with the rank of synkellos and steward, made his brother John droungarios of the Watch, their other brother Paul head of the sakellion, and the other, Constantine, genikos logothete. When Nicholas the synkellos died, they buried him in the Arkadianai, in his own house, where the metochion of Saint Constantine now stands. 11. The emperor began clearing ground near the palace to build the Nea, buying up a great many dwellings. Word was brought to the emperor that Syracuse was being besieged by the Hagarenes. Because the sailors were busy with the building of the New Church, the fleet and the men were delayed, and Syracuse was surrendered shortly before the fleet arrived, to the emperor's bitter lamentation and grief. 12. When Niketas, master of the table, son of Xylinites, was accused of being the Augusta's lover, the emperor had him tonsured and made a monk. Under the reign of Leo he became steward of the Great Church, and when he died he was laid in the monastery that he himself had built. And he cut off her [?]

13. The emperor broke up many bronze works for the sake of the New Church. He also took marbles, mosaic cubes and columns from many churches and houses for its construction. Among them was a bronze statue in the form of a bishop, holding in its hand a staff with a serpent coiled around it. They took it down and placed it [?] in the vestiarion. When the emperor came down and went to where the statue stood upright, he put his fingers into the serpent's mouth; and a living serpent that was inside bit the emperor's finger. He was cured with difficulty by antidotes, and everyone marvelled at this.

[905 Lives of the More Recent Emperors 906] 14. He also broke up the very large statue of Solomon that stood in the Basilica and ordered it to be recast in his own name and placed down in the foundations of this New Church, as though offering himself to God as a sacrifice in this building. 15. The emperor campaigned again against Melitene, took captives, won many battles, and returned. 16. The patriarch Ignatius died, and in his place the emperor raised Photius once more to be patriarch for the second time. Later, when the patriarch Photius died in exile, his body was laid in the monastery called that of Jeremiah at Merdosagaris; it had formerly been a parish church, but he himself [?] made it a convent for women. 17. Again the emperor campaigned against Germanikeia, sacked it, took captives and re-

18. Constantine died, the son of the emperor Michael by Eudokia, though, as the story goes, the son of Basil. Basil mourned him deeply, for he loved him dearly. His body was laid in the tombs of the emp-

19. On 1 May the New Church, which the emperor had built and richly adorned, was consecrated and enthroned by the patriarch Photius, the emperor wearing the loros, giving much money and naming it the Nea. 20. The emperor sent out Prokopios the protovestiarios with all the western themes, with Eupraxios as general for Sicily, Mousoulikes for Kephalenia, Rhabdouchos for Dyrrachion, and in the Peloponnese the [?] and Apostyppes. This Prokopios performed many deeds and feats of valour, but finally, when a battle took place, he was betrayed by Apostyppes and slain. 21. Leo Salibaras introduced to the patriarch Photius the monk Theodore, archbishop of Euchaita, as a pious man who worked wonders and had the gift of foresight. Photius in turn recommended him and introduced him to the emperor. The emperor was pleased with him (for he catered to the emperor's desires) and held him in great honour. When the emperor was despondent over the death of his son Constantine, because of the love he bore him, Theodore deceived him and promised to show him the boy alive; and this he did. As the emperor was passing through a thicket, a phantom on horseback met him, clad in gold-woven garments, in the likeness of Constantine. Seeing it with his own eyes, the emperor embraced and kissed it. When it vanished, he believed that he had seen his son, and as though he had not been deceived [?]. He therefore built a monastery there and named it after Saint Constantine. [?]

22. By these and other [?], being thoroughly initiated in the arts of Apollonius, the man called Santabarenos made the emperor place [?] trust in him. 23. He took the daughter of Martinakios as wife for the emperor Leo, and crowned her too, holding the wedding in the Magnaura and in the Nineteen Couches. 24. The emperor Leo was accused by Santabarenos to his father in these words: "He carries a knife, meaning to kill you with it." Yet it was Santabarenos himself who, by treacherous advice, had made Leo have this knife made and wear it in his boot, telling him: "Your father often asks for a knife for some purpose; this way you can give it to him." Leo had it made, and when he was slandered as described and caught carrying it in his boot, he defended himself at length but was not heard. So Niketas Helladikos, his protovestiarios, who became papias under the emperor Romanos, was beaten, and others with him suffered many terrible things and were exiled. The emperor confined Leo in the chamber of the Pearl and wanted to blind him, had not the patriarch Photius prevented it with many entreaties, together with Stylianos Zaoutzes, who was then small hetaireiarch. Leo spent three months out of his father's sight, weeping and lamenting, and wrote many letters [?] to the emperor. Since the emperor had great faith in Saint Elijah, Leo was presented to him [?] on the feast of Saint Elijah. When the procession took place, the people saw him and acclaimed: "Glory to you, O God!" The emperor turned and answered them: "Glorify God for my son, do you? You will have to endure many [?] from him and pass painful days." 25. Andrew, domestic of the scholai, was accused by Santabarenos of siding with Leo and was replaced by the emperor. In his place Stypiotes was appointed domestic; he went with an army to Tarsus, was defeated, and lost them all. So the emperor appointed Andrew domestic again. 26. A conspiracy was formed against the emperor by John Kourkouas, who was domestic of the Hikanatoi, after he had received an oracle from the recluse at Blachernai. Many senators and officials were found to be involved, sixty-six in all; among them were Michael the hetaireiarch, Katoudares, M[?]earis, Baboutzikos and the rest. When this plot was revealed to the emperor by the protovestiarios of Kourkouas, they were all arrested, and the emperor went out to the Hippodrome and

took his seat there, examined their cases, had them all beaten and shorn, and burned off the hair that remained. After this he went out in the procession of the Annunciation, the occasion on which they had meant to carry out the plot. As he had ordered, they walked behind him, naked and bound, as far as the Forum. Then he confiscated the property of them all and exiled them. 27. When the emperor went out to hunt, a huge stag appeared from somewhere. As the emperor was chasing it, the stag turned, caught the emperor by his belt and lifted him from his horse. Someone reached him, drew his sword, cut the belt and rescued the emperor. After his return, the emperor ordered the man who had cut his belt to be beheaded for having drawn his sword against him, though the man pleaded at length that he had done it to save his life; but it did him no good. Basil fell ill from the mauling by the stag and died, leaving Leo as autokrator, and Alexander.

THE REIGN OF LEO, SON OF BASIL. In the year 6386 of the world, and 886 of the divine Incarnation, Leo, the son of Basil, reigned for twenty-five years and eight months. His brother Stephen was a cleric and was synkellos under the patriarch Photius, who had brought him up and educated him. After becoming autokrator, Leo sent Andrew the general with many candles, clergy and senators to Chrysopolis; he brought Michael out of his tomb and placed him in a cypress-wood coffin. They laid him on a bier, covered him and honoured him as an emperor, and with hymns and great honour, his brothers also following, he brought him to the Holy Apostles and laid him in a sarcophagus. 2. After this the emperor sent Andrew, domestic of the scholai, together with John Hagiopolites, a very learned man who had been logothete of the drome. They went up into the ambo of the church, read out the charges against the patriarch Photius, deposed him from the throne, and confined him in the monastery of the Armenians called that of Bordon. 3. The emperor appointed Stylianos Zaoutzes magistros and logothete of the drome. He installed Stephen the synkellos, his brother, in the patriarchate, and before the Nativity of Christ Stephen was ordained patriarch by Theophanes the protothronos and the other bishops. After six years and five months in the patriarchate he died, and he was buried in the monastery of Sykai. 4. In the time of this Leo the fortress of Hypsele was betrayed and taken by the Hagarenes, and all who were there were taken captive. A great fire broke out near the Sophianai, and the church of the holy apostle Thomas [?] was also burned, which this same Leo splendidly restored.

[?] The emperor sent [?] and brought Theodore Santabarenos into the City. Andrew the domestic and Stephen the magistros of Kalomaria had both been heavily abused by Santabarenos in Basil's time. So they made a plot and suggested to the emperor that the patriarch Photios and Theodore Santabarenos meant to make one of Photios's own kinsmen emperor. The emperor ordered that the patriarch Photios and Theodore Santabarenos be brought to the palace at Pegai, and directed that they be kept under guard separately. The emperor sent Stephen the magistros, Andrew Krateros the domestic, the patrikios Goumer and John Hagiopolites [?] to look into the charges against them. They brought in the patriarch and seated him with honour on a throne, then sat down themselves, and Andrew the domestic said to the patriarch: "Master, do you know Abba [?] Theodore?" He answered: "Abba [?] Theodore I do not know." And Andrew said: "Do you not know Abba [?] Theodore Santabarenos?" And the patriarch said: "I know the monk Theodore, who is archbishop of Euchaita." 6. They also brought in Santabarenos [?], and Andrew the domestic said to him: "The emperor asks you this: 'Where are the money and goods of my reign?'" He said: "Wherever the emperor gave them. But now that he is looking for them, he has the authority to take them back." And Andrew said to him: "Tell me whom you [meant?] to make emperor when you plotted and urged my father to blind me: a kinsman of the patriarch, or one of your own?" He answered: "I know nothing at all about the things you are accusing me of." Then Stephen the magistros said to him: "Then how did you send word to the emperor: 'I will convict the patriarch on this'?" At once Santabarenos fell at the patriarch's feet and said: "I adjure you by God, master: first carry out my [deposition?], and then let them punish me as a criminal once I am stripped of the priesthood. For I made no such statements to the emperor." And the patriarch said in front of everyone: "By the salvation of my soul, Abba Theodore, you are an archbishop [both now?] and in the age to come." Andrew was angered at this and said: "Abba, did you not send word to the emperor through me: 'I will convict the patriarch on this'?" But he denied knowing anything. So they went back and reported to the emperor everything that had been said. The emperor was seized with rage and uncontrollable anger at finding no charge to bring against the patriarch. He sent men who beat Santabarenos severely, and he exiled him to Athens. Afterwards he sent men after him who blinded him, and he exiled him to the East. Afterwards
[?], after many entreaties, the emperor brought him back to the City and ordered that he receive provisions from the New Church. Santabarenos died in the time of Constantine and of Zoe [his mother?].

7–8. In the reign of Leo, then, Aion, the Lombard exarch and duke, who had become son-in-law of the king of Francia [?], rebelled against the emperor and brought the whole country under his own control. When the emperor learned of this, he sent Constantine, the steward of the table, with all the themes of the West to make war on Aion. When battle was joined, Constantine's men were defeated and slaughtered, and he himself barely escaped. 9. There was an eclipse of the sun, so that it became night at the sixth hour and the stars appeared. There were also thunder, gusts of wind and lightning, so that seven men were burned on the steps of the Forum. 10. The fortress of Samos was besieged by the Hagarenes, and its general Paspalas was taken captive. Emperor Leo appointed Zaoutzas basileopator, having already become intimate with his daughter Zoe after her husband Theodore Gouzouniates died by some poison. When the patriarch Stephen departed this life, Antony, called [?], was ordained in his place.

11. A report came from the general of Macedonia that Symeon, ruler of Bulgaria, intended to march against the Romans. The cause of Symeon's anger was this. Zaoutzas the basileopator had a eunuch slave named Mousikos. Mousikos became friends with Staurakios and Kosmas, men from Hellas who were merchants and lovers of gold. Out of greed for shameful gain, they used Mousikos's mediation and influence to move the Bulgarians' trade from the City to Thessalonica, and they treated the Bulgarians badly in collecting the trade duties. The Bulgarians [?] reported this to Symeon, and he informed Emperor Leo of it. But the emperor was held back by the basileopator, who favoured Mousikos, and he dismissed the whole matter as nonsense. 12. Enraged, the Bulgarian marched against the Romans. When the emperor learned of this, he sent Krenites the stratelates against the Bulgarians, with arms and many officials of the City, to oppose Symeon. Battle was joined in Macedonia and the Romans were routed. Krenites, Kourtikios the Armenian and all the rest were killed. Some of the Khazars who served in Leo's hetaireia were captured. Symeon had their noses cut off and sent them to the City to shame the Romans. When the emperor saw them he was angered, and he sent Niketas, surnamed Skleros, with dromons to the river Danube to [give?] gifts to the Turks and [stir them to?] war [?]

against Symeon. Niketas went off and met their chiefs, Arpad and Kousan. When they agreed to fight, he took hostages and came back to the emperor. The emperor then sent Eustathios, patrikios and droungarios of the fleet, by sea. He sent the patrikios Nikephoros Phokas, the domestic, with the themes by land, and Nikephoros advanced as far as the Bulgarians. After this the emperor, who welcomed peace, sent Konstantinakes the quaestor to Symeon to urge peace. But Symeon had learned of the advance against him by land and sea, and he shut the quaestor up in custody, claiming that he had come with treacherous intent. While Symeon was busy with Phokas's army, the Turks crossed over and took the whole of Bulgaria captive. When Symeon learned of this, he moved against the Turks. They crossed back and joined battle with the Bulgarians, and Symeon was routed and barely escaped to Dristra. The Turks asked the emperor to send men and buy back the Bulgarian captives. This the emperor did, sending citizens to ransom them. 13. Symeon asked for peace through Eustathios the droungarios. The emperor agreed and sent Leo Choirosphaktes to make peace. Nikephoros received orders to return with the army, and Eustathios, droungarios of the Watch, likewise. But Symeon did not deign even to speak to Leo, and kept him shut up in prison. He marched against the Turks, who had no support from the Romans to rely on but had been left with no provision made for them, and he slaughtered them all, which increased his arrogance. On his return he found Leo at Moundraga and said to him: "I will not make peace unless I receive all the captives." So the emperor ordered them to be handed over, and a Bulgarian kinsman of Symeon came with Leo and took charge of them. 14. When Nikephoros Phokas died, Symeon looked for pretexts to break the peace. Demanding still more captives, he invaded Roman territory. Emperor Leo appointed as domestic of the scholai Leo Katakalon, who had his residence at Rhaidestos [?], and sent with him Theodosios, patrikios and protovestiarios. He crossed over with all the themes and tagmata, and battle was joined with Symeon at Boulgarophygon. There was a general rout, and all perished, including the protovestiarios Theodosios, over whom the emperor grieved greatly [?]

15. In Cherson, too, the men of the fortress slaughtered their general Symeon, son of John. The fortress of Koron in Cappadocia was taken by the Hagarenes. 16. The emperor made an excursion to St Mamas [?], with Zaoutzas [the basileopator?] [?]

who held power at court, and his daughter Zoe [?], together with the emperor. The emperor's wife Theophano was not there, but was at Blachernai, praying at the Holy Soros. The emperor decided to stay there, and Zaoutzas's relatives, his son Tzaoutzes and the others, took counsel together and planned to murder the emperor in the night. Zoe was sleeping with the emperor and heard the commotion. She looked out through the window and silenced them. When she understood how terrible a plot they had devised, she woke the emperor. He at once got into a boat and crossed to Pegai, leaving Zaoutzas and all the rest there. Early in the morning he hurried into the palace, removed John, droungarios of the Watch, and appointed in his place Pardos, son of Nicholas the hetaireiarch. For Nicholas had become friends with the emperor and was revealing to him all of Zaoutzas's affairs [?], until Leo Theodotakes the magistros reconciled them. 17. The Augusta Theophano died after reigning twelve years. Not many days later God showed her to be a wonderworker, because she had been free of jealousy and had persevered unceasingly in almsgiving and in prayer to God and in the holy churches. 18. Emperor Leo crowned Zoe, daughter of Zaoutzas. Because Zoe had been accused of relations with the emperor while Theophano was still alive, the patriarch would not bless the marriage, holding it unlawful. The priest who blessed it was deposed by a synod, even though it was the emperor he had married. He was married to her by a palace cleric surnamed Sinapes. The cleric who blessed the marriage was deposed, and she reigned for one year and eight months. When Zoe died, they found a sarcophagus to lay her body in that had letters carved inside it, reading: "Daughter of Babylon, the wretched one." 19. Mousikos and Staurakios were denounced to Emperor Leo for taking gifts from the generals and officials and acting as go-betweens with the basileopator. Once Staurakios came in to Zaoutzas with letters from one of the generals. When the emperor saw him standing in the heliakon, he came up behind him, seized him by the nape of the neck and led him out, as if to ask him about the generals. He took him to the Monothyron, snatched the letters and flung them away, and handed him over to whoever happened to be there to take him out of the palace, with orders that he be tonsured. When Mousikos learned of this, he fell into despair. The emperor then went in where Mousikos was standing in attendance on Zaoutzas, [seized] him by the neck and led him out. He handed him over to Christopher the koitonites to be taken to the Stoudios monastery and made a monk. A little later Zaoutzas died

in the palace. They brought his body down, carried it off to the monastery of Kauleas and buried him there. 20. After the death of Zaoutzas, Basil the Epeiktes, son of Nicholas the hetaireiarch, became friends with Samonas the koubikoularios, a man of Hagarene origin, because he [coveted?] the imperial dignity. He confided in Samonas: "Now that our aunt Zoe is dead, the emperor is going to take another wife, and he will destroy us all. But give me your word, so that I can confide all our plans to you." Samonas gave Basil his word, and Basil confided everything to him. Samonas then went in to the emperor and said to him: "My master, I want to tell you something in private. If I tell it, I die; if I do not, you die." And he told the emperor the whole of Basil's plot. The emperor did not believe what he said, and asked: "Has someone put you up to telling me this, and have you done it for a bribe?" He replied: "My master, send trustworthy men of your choosing to my [cell?] and have them hide there. Whatever they hear from Basil and from me, let them write it down." At once the emperor sent Christopher the protovestiarios with Kalokyros the koitonites, and they went up and hid in his cell. Basil was lured in. Having received a sworn pledge from Samonas in Samonas's oratory, he told him all the details of the plot and the names of the conspirators. While they were at lunch, Christopher and Kalokyros came down and read out everything to the emperor from what they had written. At once the emperor summoned Basil and gave him twenty-four thousand miliaresia, supposedly as alms for the soul of his aunt Zoe, as she had directed, and sent him off to Macedonia. That is how he got Basil out of the City. As for the rest who had taken part and shared in the same plot, he sent Pardos, droungarios of the Watch, to Stypiotes, supposedly to fetch him, but he had first instructed Stypiotes in an imperial note to put Pardos in chains. The emperor gave out that he was going to dine at St Lazarus. At the descent of the Tzykanisterion he posted John Garidas with [?], and as the emperor was coming down, John's men seized Nicholas the hetaireiarch and took him out of the City. The emperor brought Basil back from Macedonia, interrogated and flogged him, burned off his hair, paraded him through the Mese and exiled him to Athens, where he died miserably. Likewise he dealt with Nicholas the hetaireiarch, Stylianos, John and the whole family of Zaoutzas: some he had tonsured, others he exiled, and he confiscated all their property. In this way the whole family [of Zaoutzas?] was utterly destroyed through Samonas. The emperor summoned all the magistroi and those in high office and read out in the presence

of them what Samonas had revealed, and they declared that he deserved great honour. At once the emperor honoured him with the rank of protospatharios and attached him to his own person. 22. The patriarch Antony died, and Nicholas, who was the emperor's mystikos, was ordained in his place. The fortress of Demetrias in the theme of Hellas was taken by Damian the Hagarene. 23. Emperor Leo crowned Anna, his daughter by Zoe, Zaoutzas's daughter, because the customary banquets could not be held while there was no Augusta. 24. The emperor took as his wife a very beautiful girl from the theme of Opsikion [?] named Eudokia. He crowned her, had her proclaimed and married her. She bore him a male child, [?] and both she and the child died. 25. Emperor Leo bought houses near the Holy Apostles and built there a magnificent church named after his first wife, Saint Theophano. 26. He likewise built a church, St Lazarus, at the place called Ta Topou, and made it a monastery for eunuch men. He brought there the body of St Lazarus from Cyprus and that of Mary Magdalene from Ephesus and laid them in it, and he also held the dedication of the church. While the fleet was busy with the building of these churches, Tauromenium in Sicily was taken by the Africans with great slaughter of Romans. This came about through the negligence, or rather the treachery, of Eustathios, droungarios of the fleet, and of Karamalos, who was there, and of Michael Charaktos. When they came up to the City, Michael Charaktos convicted them of treachery before the emperor and the patriarch, and they were condemned to death. But the patriarch Nicholas pleaded with the emperor, and they were spared death and made monks: Karamalos at the Pikridion and Eustathios at the Stoudios. The island of Lemnos was also taken by the Hagarenes, who carried off many captives. 27. During the procession of Mid-Pentecost, Emperor Leo went up to St Mokios and was making his entrance. As he came near the solea, a man came out from the ambo and struck him with a strong, thick staff. If the blow had not been caught by a polykandelon and weakened, it would have killed him on the spot. Blood poured from the emperor's head, and there was confusion and flight among the officials, in which many were killed. His brother Alexander had pretended to be ill and had not come down for the entrance, so that he came under suspicion of having contrived the plot. Samonas was not there either: he had gone to bring Zoe to the palace to be with the emperor. The man who struck the emperor was seized and questioned [?]. He endured many tortures and punishments

over many days without naming anyone. In the end his hands and feet were cut off and he was burned in the sphendone of the Hippodrome, and from then on that procession was abolished. 28. Some time later Mark, the very learned oikonomos of that church, came up. It was he who had completed the great Holy Saturday tetraodion of the Lord Kosmas. Dining at the emperor's table, he pleaded with the emperor not to abolish the feast. When the emperor refused, Mark said: "Master, your suffering was foretold by the prophet David. For he prophesied, saying: 'How much evil the enemy has done in your sanctuary, and how those who hate you have boasted in the midst of your feast!' And from now on, master, you are destined to hold the empire for ten years." [?] 29. Zoe, the emperor's fourth wife, was uncrowned. The emperor made an excursion to the market town of Boutios to dedicate the monastery of his protovestiarios Christopher. While he was there, news came that the Hagarene fleet was sailing up against Constantinople with the Tripolite. So the emperor sent Eustathios, droungarios of the fleet, with the whole fleet and the generals against the Tripolite. Unable to meet him in battle, they came back empty-handed. 30. So the Tripolite came and sailed in past Abydos as far as Parion. When the emperor learned of this, he fell into great despondency and distress. He sent Himerios the protasekretis as commander of the fleet against the Tripolite, but they did not dare even to come near the Hagarene fleet. By God's judgments, Leo the Tripolite himself turned back and went to Thessalonica. He besieged and took it, along with its general, Leo Chatzilakios, and carried out great slaughter and took many captives. A certain koubikoularios named Rhodophyllos had been sent to Sicily on some business, carrying a hundred pounds of gold. He happened to fall ill on the way and went into Thessalonica to bathe and recover, and there he was seized by Leo. Symeon the asekretis, who later became patrikios and protasekretis, was passing by and recovered the gold and the gifts, which Rhodophyllos had left on the road. Rhodophyllos was tortured severely and died. When the Tripolite wanted to destroy the city, Symeon learned of it and sent word to him [?] to take the gold and spare the city, and that is what happened. 31. Samonas gave out that he was going to his monastery [?] at Speira in Damatrys, but instead fled with his money and his [?], taking [?] the public horses at the relay stations. When the emperor learned of this, he sent [?]

…his [men], Basil Kamateros the hetaireiarch and George Krenites, to overtake him. As Samonas was about to cross the Halys, Nikephoros the droungarios, called Kaminas, caught up with him and would not let him cross. Samonas promised him a great deal but could not persuade him, so he took refuge at Siricha, at the precious cross, pretending that he had come out of faith in the cross. Constantine, son of Doux, caught up with him, took him along and returned to the City. The emperor ordered him to be kept under guard in the house of Bardas the Caesar. He then asked Constantine, son of Doux, about him, and on learning that Samonas really had been fleeing to Syria, he urged Doux not to say this before the senate when he questioned him there, but to say that Samonas had gone to Siricha to pray; for the emperor wished to [?] him. So he summoned Constantine, son of Doux, before the officials and said: "As you hold God and my head dear, did Samonas flee or not?" Now Doux had told the emperor beforehand that he would say what he was ordered to, provided he was not put on oath. When he heard the oaths, he declared before everyone: "He was fleeing to Syria." The emperor sent him away in anger. Samonas spent four months in the house of Bardas, and he was restored to favour [?] on the anniversary of the emperor's accession. 32. At that time a comet also appeared, sending its rays toward the East and remaining visible for forty days and nights. After his flight Samonas became a patrician. [The emperor] had a son by Zoe, his fourth wife, and at the holy Lights he was baptized by Patriarch Nicholas in the Great Church, with Emperor Alexander, Samonas the patrician and all the officials receiving him from the font. 33. At that time the Kyphe also became a home for the aged, after the courtesans had been driven out. 34. After the feast Emperor Leo was married to Zoe by Thomas the priest, who was later deposed. He proclaimed this same Zoe Augusta, and for this the patriarch barred the emperor from entering the church. So he would pass along the right side as far as the mitatorion, and never went through in the customary way. 35. Samonas was promoted parakoimomenos because he was the emperor's accomplice in every lawlessness and wickedness. And they began to plot against the Church. On the first of February they summoned Patriarch Nicholas and pleaded with him at length to accept the polygamy. When they could not persuade him, they took him from the kletorion through the Boukoleon, put him in a small boat and ferried him across to

Hieria. From there he made his way on foot to Galakrenai with great difficulty, for deep snow lay on the ground. In his place Euthymios the synkellos was ordained patriarch, a man fit for the priesthood, self-controlled and very devout. They say he accepted this office because of a divine revelation, since the emperor was planning to establish a heresy and a law allowing a man to have three or even four wives, and many highly learned men were helping him in this. 36. In June Emperor Leo was invited by Constantine Lips to the monastery at Mardosangares to perform its dedication and to dine. And a wind called Lips [?] arose and blew violently until the third hour, shaking and rocking houses and churches, so that everyone fled into the open, saying it was the end of the world. And so it would have been, had not God's love for mankind stopped the destruction with rain. 37. When the fleet of the Hagarenes sailed out against the Romans, the emperor appointed Himerios, logothete of the drome, commander of all the naval forces. Andronikos Doux also received orders to join Himerios the logothete on the ships and make war on the Hagarenes. But Samonas was Andronikos's implacable enemy. Ever since his flight he had continually schemed and plotted against him, contriving by every means and with all his zeal to do Andronikos harm. He prompted someone to write secretly to Andronikos: "Do not board the ships, or you will be seized by Himerios; for Samonas has suggested to the emperor that you be seized and blinded by him." So although Himerios urged him repeatedly to embark against the Hagarenes, Andronikos balked. As the Hagarenes pressed on, Himerios engaged them alone on the day of Saint Thomas and won a great victory. When Andronikos learned of this, he despaired, and went off with his relatives, his children and his men and seized the fortress of Kabala, breaking into open rebellion. Samonas even said to the emperor: "Did I not tell you, master, that Doux was a rebel?" 38. The emperor at once sent Gregory the Iberitzes, domestic of the scholai, who was Andronikos's co-father-in-law, to make war on him. When Andronikos learned of this, and that Patriarch Nicholas had been driven out, he fled to the Hagarenes, who had then come out against the Romans, together with his relatives, friends and children, and he was received with great honour by the caliph. 39. Emperor Leo grieved over Andronikos and often wanted to send him a signed pledge of safety, as Theophilos had done for Manuel. Some advised the emperor to show favour to one of the [?] of the Praetorium and to have him

sent to Syria with a signed pledge. The emperor did so, writing in cinnabar and sending it with a golden seal inside a short roll [?]. When the Hagarene left the emperor, Samonas summoned him and said: "Do you know what you are carrying?" Having said this, [?] the wax: "You are carrying the ruin of Syria." And he gave it to him and instructed him to put it into the hands of the vizier. The man went and did so. Andronikos was seized and imprisoned with all his relatives. Learning that this had happened to him through Samonas's treachery, he was forced to become a Muslim, he and those with him. After that, his son Constantine and the rest, seeing that Andronikos could not possibly get out, took flight on his advice not long afterward and, remarkably, escaped from the heart of Syria to Roman territory. They were attacked from one region to the next, and only a few, with his son Constantine, barely came through safely. 40. From Tarsus old Abalbakes and Samonas's father came to the City about an exchange of prisoners, and the emperor received them in the Magnaura with ceremony, honour and splendour. They also decked out the Great Church with costly ornaments and showed all the precious vessels to the Hagarenes, which was unworthy of the empire and of the Christian order, that the sacred vessels of God should be seen by the heathen. Samonas's father wanted to be with his son and stay in Roman territory. But Samonas advised him: "Keep the faith you have; and I, if I can, will rather come to you." 41. On the day of Pentecost Emperor Leo had his son Constantine crowned by Patriarch Euthymios. Samonas gave Constantine, a man of his who had formerly served Basil the magistros and keeper of the inkstand, to serve Zoe Augusta. He became a favourite of Emperor Leo and the Augusta. For this reason Samonas grew very jealous of him and slandered him as having relations with the Augusta. The emperor believed this was true and sent and had him tonsured a monk in the monastery of Saint Tarasios through Samonas. But shortly afterward he ordered Samonas to take him into his own monastery at Speira, since he wanted to take him back again. So, going out on an excursion to Damatrys and dining at Samonas's monastery, he saw Constantine and at once gave Samonas his orders. Samonas dressed him in lay clothes, Constantine poured the emperor's wine at the banquet, and he returned with him to the palace. 42. Seeing the emperor's affection for him growing, Samonas plotted with the chief koitonites and Michael Tzirithon, and they drew up a paper full of abuse against the emperor, Rhodios the notary writing and composing it

[?] of Samonas. When the emperor came to the Great Church, he found it in the mitatorion, at the place where he prayed. He picked it up, and on reading it he was in great distress and sought out the one who had done it. There was also an eclipse of the moon, and the emperor ordered the astronomers of the day to declare what it portended. As Pantaleon the metropolitan, a friend of Samonas, was going in to the emperor, Samonas asked him: "Whom does the misfortune threaten?" The metropolitan told him: "You. But if you get past the thirteenth of June, you will suffer no harm after that." To the emperor, however, he said that the moon portended misfortune for the second [in rank]; and the emperor took this to mean his brother Alexander. After this Tzirithon told the emperor privately: "Samonas made the pamphlet." At once the emperor sent Samonas down to his house, had him tonsured a monk and taken to the monastery of Patriarch Euthymios. Later, when he was slandered again, he had him taken to the monastery of Martinakes. He made Constantine parakoimomenos and built a monastery for him at Nosiai, and went with Patriarch Euthymios and they dedicated it

43. In October there was a naval battle between Himerios the logothete and Damian and Leo the Hagarene, while Romanos, who later became emperor, was strategos of Samos. Himerios was defeated and barely escaped, and almost everyone there was in danger.

44. Emperor Leo began to suffer from an intestinal illness, so that he could not go out to the Magnaura to deliver the address at the beginning of the fasts. There was also a fire in the candle workshops of the Great Church, in which all the archives and the sakelle were burned. In May Leo died, having named his brother Alexander emperor. When he saw him coming to him, they say, he said: "Behold the evil time after thirteen months," and he pleaded with him earnestly and begged him to protect his son Constantine. And the emperor's word came true, for Alexander did indeed die after thirteen months. THE REIGN OF ALEXANDER, SON OF BASIL. 1. In the year of the world 6412, and of the divine incarnation [?], Alexander, son of Basil, reigned for one year and twenty-nine days, together with Constantine, son of Leo. He sent and brought Nicholas back from Galakrenai, deposed Patriarch Euthymios, and enthroned the same Nicholas as patriarch a second time. Alexander held a silention and a synod in the Magnaura, bringing Euthymios from the Stenon, from the monastery of Agathos. Sitting together with Patriarch Nicholas they carried out his deposition, shamefully plucking out the venerable beard of this holy and [?]

man, and inflicting certain other [?] and punishments on him, which the venerable and holy man endured quietly and meekly. [?] He was banished again to the monastery of Agathos, where he died, and he is buried in his own monastery in the City at Psamathia. 2. Because of the suspicions his brother Leo had held against him while he was still alive, this Alexander always spent his time hunting and on pursuits outside the palace, doing none of an emperor's work, but living in luxury, debauchery and drunkenness, and always given over to these things. So when he came to rule himself he did nothing noble, but at once made John the priest, surnamed Lazares, rhaiktor. This man ended his life wretchedly after Alexander's death while playing ball at the Hebdomon. Likewise he made Gabrielopoulos and Basilitzes, who were of the Slav nation, extremely rich from the palace treasury. It is said that, being childless, he even wanted to make this Basil emperor and to castrate Constantine, son of Leo. He intended this many times, but was thwarted by those who had received favours from Leo, who suggested now that the boy was an infant, now that he was sickly. 3. In his time a comet appeared in the West for fifteen days. They said it was called xiphias, the swordfish, and that it would bring bloodshed to the City. 4. He gave himself over to deceivers and sorcerers, who made him out to be the talisman of a wild boar [?], "bound up with you and your life," hinting that the foolish man was a little pig. Deceived by them, he restored the boar's genitals and tusks, as though they were missing. Trusting in the same delusion, he held races, took the [?] and chandeliers of the churches, decorated the hippodrome with them, and lit up the statues. For this the hand of God [?] him, as one who had given God's honour to idols. 5. When Himerios the logothete returned from the defeat by the Hagarenes, Alexander sent and confined him in the palace monastery called Kalypta, threatening him as one who had been his enemy in the time of his brother Leo. Overcome by great distress [?], he died after six months of confinement. 6. Symeon, the ruler of Bulgaria, sent to Alexander proposing peace, and asking to be treated with friendship and honour as he had been under Leo. But Alexander, gripped by folly and senselessness, sent the envoys away in disgrace and terrified Symeon with threats.
So when the peace was thus [?] broken, Symeon prepared to move against the Christians.

7. After he had dined and [?], Alexander was struck by a blow from heaven. He went up [to the palace], and with much blood pouring from his nose and genitals he died two days later. He left as guardians Patriarch Nicholas, Stephen the magistros, John Eladas, John the rhaiktor, Euthymios, Basilitzes and Gabrielopoulos, and bequeathed the empire to his nephew Constantine, son of Emperor Leo. They laid Alexander to rest in the tombs with his father.

THE REIGN OF CONSTANTINE, SON OF LEO. 1. When his father died, Constantine was still a boy (he was in the seventh year of his age), and he had been left on the throne by his uncle Alexander under guardians. He reigned under his guardians, with his mother, for another seven years; together with his father-in-law Romanos, in a subordinate position, for another twenty-six years; and as sole ruler for fifteen years, so that the whole length of his reign was 55 years. Patriarch Nicholas took control of the palace, since he too was a guardian along with Stephen the magistros and John Eladas, also a magistros, and he looked after the public welfare and took charge of the affairs of the empire day by day. 2. While the empire was in this condition, Constantine Doux, who was domestic of the scholai, received word from some of the magnates in the City, who admired him as brave and sensible and able to govern the empire well, to come in and take control of it without effort. Since he had long dreamed of this and had always coveted the [?], he reached the imperial city as quickly as he could with a considerable number of notable men. Entering by night through a postern gate belonging to Michael the protovestiarios, near the acropolis, he spent the night without sleep with his companions in the house of his father-in-law Gregoras. Niketas the asekretis, who later became protonotarios, reported Constantine's arrival to the patrician and monk Constantine Helladikos, and both came to Constantine Doux that same night. They took counsel, and before daybreak, while it was still dark, they seized the gate of the hippodrome with torches, a large crowd and weapons, acclaiming Constantine as emperor. There his groom was speared and killed by those inside the gates of the hippodrome. 3. So Constantine was not admitted but driven back. As if driven into frenzy by some demon, and with his reason unsettled by his lust for the [?], he withdrew from the hippodrome gloomy and

[?]. From there, amid acclamations, he came to the place called the Chalke, and entering through the Iron Gate of the Chalke he reached the Exkoubitoi. Then John Eladas the magistros picked out men from the hetaireia and the oarsmen and sent them armed against Doux. When they reached the Chalke and the fighting began, many fell on both sides, so many that the place became a pool of blood flowing like a river. Gregoras, Doux's son, was also killed, as were his cousin Michael and the well-known Kourtikes, the Armenian. 4. When Constantine Doux learned this, in the utter confusion that followed, he spurred on his horse. But it slipped on the paving slabs there and threw its rider to the ground. Someone caught him lying on the ground (for all the others had scattered) and cut off his head with a sword. 5. When these things had been done, Gregoras the magistros, his father-in-law, together with Leo, whom they called Choirosphaktes, took refuge in God's holy Great Church. They dragged them out of there by force and tonsured them as monks in the monastery of Stoudios. Constantine Helladikos they flogged with ox-hide whips, dressed in rags, set on a donkey and paraded through the middle of the City; then they took him to the monastery of Dalmatos and shut him up in the cell called Katadike. Leo Katakalitzes and Abessalom, son of Arotras, they blinded and sent into exile. Constantine, son of Eulampios, and others with him were beheaded by Theophilos the eparch, son of Lampoudes, in the sphendone of the hippodrome. They searched hard for Niketas the asekretis and Constantine Lips, but did not find them, since they had fled. As for the notorious Aigides and those with him, who were brave and numerous, they impaled them all on double stakes from the Damalis at Chrysopolis as far as Leukates. And these so-called guardians would have put many of the officials of the time to death mercilessly and without cause, had not some of the judges restrained them from their unjust impulse, saying to them: "Since the emperor is a child, how do you dare do such things without his command?" They tonsured Doux's wife and sent her away to her own house in Paphlagonia, and they also castrated her son Stephen. 6. 7. In August Symeon, the Bulgarian ruler, campaigned against the Romans with a great and formidable host and reached Constantinople. He laid siege to it and built a palisade around it from Blachernai to the so-called Golden Gate, buoyed up by hopes of taking it without any effort at all. But when he learned how strong the walls were, and how secure the city was through the number of its defenders and its stone-throwers, his hopes were dashed, and he came to the [?]

…he went back to the place called the Hebdomon, asking for a peace treaty. The regents accepted the peace with great eagerness, and Symeon sent Theodore the magistros to discuss the terms of peace. Then the patriarch Nicholas and the magistroi Stephen and John took the emperor with them and came to Blachernae. They brought in Symeon's two sons, who dined with the emperor in the palace. The patriarch Nicholas went out to Symeon, and Symeon bowed his head to him. The patriarch said a prayer and then, as they say, placed his own veil on Symeon's head in place of a crown. Symeon and his sons were honoured with countless magnificent gifts and returned to their own country, though they parted without agreeing on the peace. 8. Emperor Constantine was still a child and kept asking for his mother, for Emperor Alexander had already driven her out of the palace, as has been said. So [?] they brought her back up to the palace. Once she had taken control of the government, she brought up to the palace Constantine the parakoimomenos, and Constantine and Anastasius, who were called the Gongylioi. On the advice of John Eladas she removed Emperor Alexander's intimates: John the rhaiktor, the man called Gabrielopoulos, Basilitzes and the rest. The Augusta Zoe also appointed Theophylact Domenicus as hetaireiarch. John Eladas the magistros fell ill, and the doctors gave him up. He came down from the palace and went to Blachernae, where his illness got worse and he died. On the advice of Domenicus the hetaireiarch, Zoe angrily removed the patriarch Nicholas together with his associates, [telling him] to look after the affairs of his own church and take care of

9. Not long afterward Constantine the parakoimomenos accused Domenicus the hetaireiarch before the Augusta, saying that he was trying to get the throne for his own brother. As a pretext they made him a patrikios. Then, when he went down to the church to receive the blessing as was customary, they ordered him to stay at home. Zoe appointed John Garidas as hetaireiarch and the eunuch Damian as droungarios of the Watch. Domenicus went off to his house, lamenting to no purpose. 10. Symeon the Bulgarian was plundering Thrace again, and the Augusta and the high officials were concerned about how to put a stop to his arrogance. Then John Bogas asked to be made a patrikios and promised to bring the Pechenegs against him. His request was granted and he received gifts. He went to the land of the Pechenegs, made a treaty, took hostages from there and brought them to the City, while the Pechenegs agreed to cross over and make war on Symeon. 11. Ashot also came to the City. He was a man very famous for his strength and was the son of the prince of

princes. They say that he could take hold of an iron rod by its ends with both hands and use his enormous strength to bend it into a circle, so that the stubborn nature of the iron gave way to the force of his hands. When he arrived they received him with great honour, and [sent him] back to his own country [?].

12. In the month of September of the third indiction, Pankratoukas the Armenian surrendered Adrianople to Symeon. Not long afterward Zoe sent Basil, patrikios and kanikleios, and Niketas Helladikos, protospatharios, with many gifts, and they recovered the city. 13. The emir Damian also came with ships to attack Strobilos with a large force. He would have taken it, except that he fell ill and died, and the Hagarenes went back empty-handed. 14. The inhabitants of Hellas and Athens were constantly abused by Chase, the son of Judah, and they could no longer bear his debauchery. So they stoned him to a miserable death inside the sanctuary of the church at Athens. 15. The Augusta Zoe saw Symeon's arrogance and his attacks on the Christians, and she decided with the high officials to arrange a prisoner exchange and peace with the Hagarenes, and then to bring the whole army of the East across to make war on Symeon and destroy him. So the patrikios John Rhadinos and Michael Toxaras were sent to Syria to carry out the exchange. When this was done, they made the customary distribution of pay to the tagmata, took them along with the themes and crossed into the region of Thrace. The domestic of the Schools at that time was Leo Phokas the magistros, a man who had courage rather than the judgement needed for command. Constantine, protopapas of the palace, who was called Kephalas, and Constantine Malelias brought the venerable and life-giving wood of the Cross out into Thrace. All the soldiers venerated it and swore to die alongside one another, and then the whole army set out against the Bulgarians. John Grapson commanded the tagma of the Excubitors, and the son of Maroules commanded the Hikanatoi. Romanos Argyros was a general, as were his brother Leo and Bardas Phokas. Melias was with them with the Armenians, along with all the other generals of the themes. Also present with the rest was the patrikios Constantine Lips, who advised Leo the domestic in all matters. 17. On the 20th of the month of August, in the fifth indiction, the battle between the Bulgarians and the Romans was fought at the river Achelous. And (since the judgements of God are unsearchable and beyond tracing) the whole Roman army was routed. There was a complete rout and dreadful wailing. Some were trampled by one another,

others were killed by the enemy, and there was such bloodshed as had never happened since the beginning of time. Leo the domestic fled and reached safety in Mesembria. Among the others who were slaughtered in that clash were Constantine Lips, John Grapson and a large number of other commanders. 17. At that time the patrikios Romanos, who was droungarios of the fleet, was also sent with the whole fleet to the river Danube to help Leo Phokas. John Bogas was likewise sent to bring the Pechenegs down, as was said before, and the droungarios Romanos was ordered to ferry them across against the Bulgarians so that they could fight alongside Leo Phokas. But Romanos and John Bogas fell into quarrels and disputes, and when the Pechenegs saw them fighting and feuding with each other, they withdrew to their own land. 18. When the war was over and Romanos and Bogas had returned to the City, proceedings were begun against them. The droungarios Romanos was put in such danger that a sentence of condemnation was passed, that he should be deprived of his eyes. The charge was that through negligence, or rather through malice, he had not ferried the Pechenegs across but had withdrawn too soon, and had not even taken the fleeing Romans onto his ships. He would have suffered this if the sentence had not been overturned by Constantine Gongylios and Stephen the magistros, who had great influence with the Augusta. 19. Then the Bulgarians, elated by their victory, campaigned as far as the City. Leo the domestic of the Schools, John the hetaireiarch and Nicholas the son of Doux went out against the Bulgarians with a very large force to a place in Thrace called Katasyrtai. During the night the Bulgarians fell on them unexpectedly. The domestic fled, and Nicholas the son of Doux was killed together with many others. 20. Theodore, the tutor of Emperor Constantine, saw that Constantine the parakoimomenos was trying to get the throne for his own brother-in-law Leo. So he suggested to Emperor Constantine that he take on the droungarios Romanos, since Romanos had been his father's servant and was loyal to him. That way Romanos could be with him and guard him, and the emperor would have an ally and helper in whatever he might need. Romanos was approached about this many times and refused. So Emperor Constantine wrote a document in his own hand, made it binding with his writing and signature, and sent it to him. When Romanos had it in his hands, he promised to make his move against Constantine the parakoimomenos and his relatives in the following way. 21. As this rumour was spreading, Constantine the parakoimomenos kept pressing Romanos to set out with the fleet. Romanos pleaded that he could not sail away because the fleet had not [?]

received its customary pay. While Romanos was fitting out and preparing the ships, Constantine the parakoimomenos went out to hurry him into sailing. Romanos met him with the manner of a servant and promised to do as he was told with all eagerness. When the parakoimomenos wanted to go back, he asked Romanos whether he had handsome, brave men to row the imperial trireme. Romanos at once signalled with his hand to men who were standing ready to come near. They knew the plan and were already very close to Romanos's dromon. Walking behind Constantine the parakoimomenos, Romanos called out, 'Seize him and carry him off!' They seized him at once, took him into the trireme of the droungarios Romanos and kept him under guard. No one defended the man or showed him any pity, since everyone who was with him ran away. 22. When the Augusta Zoe learned of this, she summoned the patriarch Nicholas and her magnates and sent them to Romanos to find out what had happened. When they crossed over, the people pelted them with stones and drove them away. At dawn Zoe came out onto the terrace of the Boukoleon and called out to her son and to everyone, 'How has this rebellion happened?' Theodore, the tutor of Emperor Constantine, answered her, 'These things have happened because Leo Phokas has ruined [?] the Romans and Constantine the parakoimomenos has ruined the palace.' 23. The emperor brought the patriarch Nicholas and Stephen the magistros to be with him in the palace, taking power from his mother into his own hands. The next day he sent John Toubakes to remove the Augusta Zoe from the palace. But with wailing and tears she clung to her son and moved him to pity and compassion for his mother, so that the emperor said, 'Let my mother stay with me.' And as soon as he said this they let her go. 24. The emperor and the patriarch summoned John Garidas and appointed him domestic of the Schools, since they were afraid that Leo Phokas might turn to rebellion. But he would not agree to this unless they appointed his brother-in-law Theodore Zouphinezer, and Symeon his son, as hetaireiarch. Once they had assured him with oaths, he went down to his house. Then they immediately removed his relatives from the palace. When these relatives came to him and he saw them, he was seized with trembling and horror and was beside himself. So he went straight out to Romanos and told him what he had suffered. He made friends with him, and they gave and received oaths so that the two of them would have

one soul. He became one in mind and spirit with Romanos, so that they even agreed to make a marriage alliance and so tighten the bond of friendship further. 25. On the 24th of March Romanos sent John the presbyter, a close and very trusted friend of his, and Theodore, who was called Matzoukes, to the palace to plead his case: 'What I have done was not a rebellion. I was guarding against an attack by Phokas and was afraid that he might attempt some revolt against the emperor. That is why I have decided to go up to the palace and act as the emperor's guard.' Since the patriarch Nicholas did not agree to this, the tutor mentioned above sent word to Romanos to come to the Boukoleon with the whole fleet. Romanos consulted with his men (for fate was leading him on), and on the day of the Annunciation of the most holy Theotokos (it was a Thursday) he came armed to the Boukoleon with the whole fleet. Stephen the magistros left the palace at once, and the patrikios Niketas, whose child had married a child of Romanos, went up to the palace and brought the patriarch Nicholas out of it. The people of the palace received oaths of assurance from Romanos and sent him the precious Cross. He venerated it, gave them his oath, and went up to the palace with them and a few others. He made obeisance to the emperor, went with him into the church in the Pharos and gave him pledges of loyalty. The emperor at once appointed him magistros and great hetaireiarch. 27. An imperial order was immediately sent to Leo Phokas, instructing him not to think of any sedition at all but to rest for a while in his own house. Letters were likewise ordered to be written to Constantine the parakoimomenos with similar instructions, that he should plot nothing hostile but submit to Emperor Constantine. Andrew, primikerios of the imperial wardrobe, took these letters and delivered them to him while he was at [?]. He received them, read them, went off to his own house and kept quiet. 27. In the fifth week of the holy Fast, Emperor Constantine gave a pledge of betrothal to Helena, the daughter of Romanos. On the third day of Easter, which is called the day of Galilee, the patriarch Nicholas blessed their marriage and crowned him together with her. 28. The emperor appointed Romanos basileopator and made Romanos's son Christopher hetaireiarch in his place. Not long afterward Leo Phokas was misled by some officials and by his own tagmata and was stirred to rebellion. He sent for and brought to his side Constantine the parakoimomenos and Constantine and Anastasius, the [?]

Gongylioi brothers, and Constantine Malelias the protasekretis. He assured them all and insisted that he was starting this movement on behalf of Emperor Constantine. But Romanos the basileopator drew up signed chrysobulls in the name of Emperor Constantine. They overturned this plot and declared that those who abandoned Phokas and took refuge with the emperor were on the emperor's side. He gave them to a shameless, bold woman named Anna and to a cleric named Michael and sent them into Phokas's camp. They took the documents and spread them through the whole army. Michael was caught by Phokas, mercilessly beaten, and had his nose and ears cut off. Afterwards Romanos gave him a fitting reward, and he did the same for the woman who had been sent with him.

29. The first to leave Phokas and run over to Romanos was Constantine, son of Michael Bareus, and this was the beginning of the collapse of the rebellion and usurpation. With him came Balantios and the man called Atzmoros, both tourmarchs. Leo Phokas reached Chrysopolis with a very large, heavily armed force and drew up battle lines from the stone Heifer as far as Chalcedon to frighten the people in the City. So Romanos sent Symeon, the official of the kanikleion, with a dromon. Symeon carried a signed statement from Emperor Constantine, which said: 30. 'I have found no one among my subjects to be a more watchful, loyal and faithful guardian of my reign than Romanos. So, after God, I have entrusted my protection to him and decided to regard him as a father, since he has shown me a father's affection and a parent's care. As for this Leo Phokas, I always suspected him of plotting against my reign, and now his own actions have shown that he is a plotter and is rising up against my rule like a usurper. Therefore I do not wish him to be domestic from now on. I declare that he did not start this rebellion with my approval, but that he made this attack of his own accord, trying to seize the throne for himself.' When this was read out to the troops, they all began to withdraw and go over to the basileopator Romanos. Phokas found himself helpless and gave up, as a man who had lost all hope. He fled and came to the fortress of Ateous [?], but was not let in. Romanos then sent John Toubakes and Leo, his relative, to bring him into the City. They seized him and blinded him, although they had received no orders about it. They did it

of their own accord, so that even the basileopator Romanos was angry about it. 31. In the month of August a plot by Constantine Ktematinos, David Kamoulianos and Michael, curator of the Mangana, was reported. They were beaten, their property was confiscated, they were paraded through the middle of the City, and they were sent into exile. Leo, the magistros and domestic of the Schools, was also brought into the City and led through the middle of the marketplace, sitting on a mule. 32–33. The Augusta Zoe was also caught plotting against Romanos with poisoned food prepared by Theokletos, notary of the service department. They removed her from the palace and took her to Petrion, where she was tonsured in the monastery of Saint Euphemia. 34. Theophylact, patrikios and count of the stable, invited Theodore, the tutor of Emperor Constantine, and his brother Symeon to lunch. While they were eating, John, droungarios of the Watch, who was called Kourkouas, came in with a large force. He seized them and exiled them to the Opsikion, to their own estates, on the charge that they were plotting against Romanos. 35. On the 24th of the month of September Romanos was honoured with the rank of Caesar. On the 17th of the month of December, the Sunday of the Fathers, he was crowned with the imperial diadem by Emperor Constantine, his son-in-law, and the patriarch Nicholas. On the 6th of January, the day of the Holy Lights, he crowned his wife Theodora. On the 17th of the month of May, in the fifth indiction, Romanos's son Christopher was proclaimed emperor. Emperor Constantine crowned him on the 24th of the same month, the day of Holy Pentecost, and those two alone went out in that procession. 1–2. In the month of June of the eighth indiction, on a Sunday, Romanos brought about the reunion of the Church. Everyone was reunited, both metropolitans and clergy, who had been split between the patriarch Nicholas and Euthymius. 3. On the 8th of the month of February, in the ninth indiction, Romanos sent the magistros Stephen, son of Kalomaria, into exile on the island of Antigone, because he had been accused of aiming at the throne. Romanos had him tonsured as a monk, together with Theophanes Teichiotes and Paul the Orphanotrophos, men

4. Emperor Romanos held a procession at the Tribunal, and everyone had gathered there under arms. While the muster was going on, Romanos and Constantine suddenly hurried back to the palace. Leo, one of Arsenios's men, had reported a plot by Arsenios himself and Paul the manglabites. They were beaten, their property was confiscated, and they were exiled. At that time John the presbyter, the rhaiktor, held power at the emperor's side.

[?] He made Leo, the son of Arsenios, hebdomadarios, bringing him into close attachment to the emperor.
5. There was in Hellas a certain Rentakios, a relative of the patrician Niketas. He was uneducated and a parricide. He pursued his own father to murder him, but the father fled the attack, boarded a ship, sailed away and was captured by the Cretans. Finding himself unhindered, this Rentakios plundered all his father's property. He then came up to the City and took refuge in the Great Church of God. When the emperor Romanos learned of his lawlessness and plundering, he resolved to remove him from the church and punish him. Rentakios, however, forged letters to the Bulgarians and planned to desert to them. He was caught and convicted, and was deprived of his eyes.
6. The Bulgarians again marched out as far as Katasyrtai. After the death of the domestic Adralestos, Pothos Argyros was appointed domestic of the Schools. He went out with the tagmata as far as Thermopolis and sent Michael, the son of Moroleon, who was a topoteretes, to spy on the Bulgarians. Michael unexpectedly came right into their troop and killed many of the Bulgarians, but he was himself wounded, and after entering the City he died.
7. At that time Theokletos, a notary of the service, revealed a plot against the emperor Romanos. It was formed by Anastasios, the sakellarios and head of the goldsmiths' workshop, by Theodoretos the koitonites, Demetrios the imperial notary of the eidikon, Nicholas Koubatzes and Theodotos the protokarabos, who were supposedly working on behalf of the emperor Constantine. They were convicted, flogged, paraded along the Mese and sent into exile. Theodoretos was flogged separately in the part of the palace called the Trikonchos, and he too was exiled. The sakellarios Anastasios was tonsured in the monastery of the Elegmoi, where he also died. Seizing on this pretext, Romanos demoted the emperor Constantine to second place and advanced himself to first place.
8. Symeon again campaigned against the Romans. He sent large numbers of Bulgarians under Kaukanos, Minikos[?] and others, with orders to drive on the City as fast as possible. They crossed the mountains and came as far as [?]. When the emperor Romanos learned of their approach, he feared that they would come down and burn the palaces at Pegai and the Stenon. So he sent John the rhaiktor together with Leo and Pothos, known as the Argyroi, with a sizable force drawn from the imperial troops, the hetaireia and the tagmata. With them was also Alexios Mosele, patrician and droungarios of the fleet, with his men. It was the fifth week of Lent. They drew up their troops in the

level, low-lying ground at Pegai. The Bulgarians appeared above them in arms, raised a wild and terrifying war cry and charged them with great violence. John the rhaiktor fled at once. Photeinos, the son of Platypous, was cut down fighting to protect him, and many others with him. John was barely rescued and got aboard the dromon. Alexios Mousele the droungarios also came fleeing to the dromon in his armour, but he could not climb the dromon's ladder. He fell into the sea with his protomandator and drowned. The Argyroi fled into the little fort and were saved. Of the marines and the whole remaining host, some fled the enemy's hands and drowned in the sea, some fell to the sword, and some were taken captive by the Bulgarians. With no one to stop them, the Bulgarians set fire to the palaces at Pegai and burned the whole Stenon. So terrible a thing is bad counsel, and inexperience allied with rashness.
10. On the twentieth of February, in the tenth indiction, Theodora, the wife of Romanos, died. Her body was laid in the emperor Romanos's own house, which he had converted into a monastery.
11. In the same month Sophia, the wife of the emperor Christopher, was crowned. At that time the kouropalates of Iberia also came to the City. He passed through the middle of the marketplace, which had been splendidly decorated, and was received with great glory and honour. They also brought him into God's Hagia Sophia to see its beauty and size and its costly adornment. They had decorated it, hung it with gold-woven cloths and every kind of ornament, and then brought him inside. He was astounded at the marvellous and enormous structure of the church and greatly admired its costly adornment. He said that this place was truly the dwelling of God, and then returned to his [?]

12. In the month of June the Bulgarians campaigned again. They came as far as the palaces of Saint Theodora and set them on fire. The emperor Romanos invited the commanders of the tagmata to a meal, and the man called Saktikes was with them. He exhorted them and urged them to go out against the enemy and fight for their country. They readily agreed to die for his majesty and for the Christians. The next day the aforementioned Saktikes was armed by the emperor and proved that his loyalty and courage were genuine. He got behind the Bulgarians, fell upon their camp and slaughtered everyone he found there. When the Bulgarians learned what had happened, they returned to their camp. Battle was joined, and they routed Saktikes, who had only a few men with him. Since he

had fought nobly and killed many but could no longer hold out against the enemy's numbers, he gave his horse its head and rode off in flight. As he was crossing a river that flowed nearby, his horse stuck fast in the mud, and he was wounded in the buttock and the thigh. With the help of his men the horse was barely dragged out of the mire, and he got safely to Blachernae, where he was laid in the holy Soros. The wound was mortal, and he died that night.
13. At that time the most reverend Petronas, at the command of the emperor Romanos, brought a sarcophagus carved with figures and two others without carving from the monastery for men of Saint Mamas, which is near the gate called Xylokerkos. They say that Maurice lay in them with his sons. These were placed in the emperor's monastery, that is, the Myrelaion.
14. A certain Adrian the Chaldian, together with Tzantzes, a very wealthy Armenian, plotted a usurpation and revolt against the emperor Romanos. They acted at the instigation and on the advice of Bardas Boilas, who was strategos in Chaldia, and seized the fortress called Paiperte. John Kourkouas, the domestic of the Schools, defeated them and captured some of them. He blinded the more prominent ones and confiscated their property, but he ordered that the poor and obscure should go free wherever they wished. Tzantzes escaped to another very strong fort, received a pledge of immunity and came into the City. He was honoured with the rank of manglabites and lived in honour in the house of the Mangana. But he plotted to escape, was caught and was deprived of his eyes. Bardas Boilas was tonsured a monk, because the emperor took pity on him as a friend.
15. The patrician called Moroleon was strategos of Adrianople. He was a very able and skilful man and had performed many feats of bravery against the Bulgarians. The Bulgarian Symeon again surrounded that city with his whole army. The grain in the city ran out and a severe famine pressed hard on its people, for they had no way of getting supplies from anywhere. Driven by want, they surrendered themselves and the strategos to the Bulgarians. Symeon seized him, bound his whole body in chains and punished him with countless tortures. At last he killed him with a bitter death, worthy of Symeon's own most harsh and cruel soul. Then he handed the city over to Bulgarians to guard and withdrew. When they heard that the Roman army was advancing against them, they abandoned it and left, and it came under the Romans again.
16. Leo of Tripoli set out against the Romans with a large force and warships and reached the island of Lemnos. John,

called Rhadenos, patrician and droungarios of the fleet, suddenly attacked him and reached the island. A battle followed, and with God's help the Hagarenes under Leo were routed. [?] Leo of Tripoli saved himself by flight.
17. In the month of September, in the second indiction, Symeon, the ruler of Bulgaria, campaigned against Constantinople with his whole army. He plundered Thrace and Macedonia, burning and laying waste everything and cutting down the trees. When he reached Blachernae, he demanded that the patriarch Nicholas and some of the magnates be sent to him to negotiate peace. Both sides took hostages from each other. First the patriarch went out, then the patrician Michael, called Stypiotes, and John, the mystikos and paradynasteuon. John the rhaiktor had by then been slandered to the emperor. He had pleaded illness, left the palace and been tonsured in his monastery near Galakrenai.
18. These men discussed peace with Symeon, but he sent them away and asked to see the emperor Romanos himself. Many people had told him about the emperor's prudence, courage and intelligence. The emperor was delighted at this, for he longed for peace and for an end to the bloodshed that happened every day. He sent men to the shore at Kosmidion and had a very strong landing stage built out into the sea, so that the imperial trireme could sail up and moor there. He had it fenced in on every side and ordered a dividing wall to be built across the middle, where the two of them were to talk with each other. Symeon, however, sent men and burned the church of the most holy Theotokos at Pege and everything around it. This made it plain that he did not want peace but was deceiving the emperor with empty hopes.
19. The emperor went to Blachernae with the patriarch Nicholas. He entered the holy Soros and stretched out his hands in prayer. Then he fell face down and wet that holy floor with his tears. He begged the all-immaculate Theotokos to soften the unbending and implacable heart of the arrogant tyrant Symeon and persuade him to agree to peace. They opened the holy casket where the venerable omophorion of the most holy Theotokos was kept, and the emperor took it out. He put it on like an unbreakable breastplate, and put on his faith in the blameless Theotokos like a helmet. So he left the church protected by sure armour. He equipped the fleet that was with him with shields and sure weapons and reached the place appointed for the meeting [?]

Symeon came with a countless host, divided into many units. Some had golden shields and golden spears, others silver shields and silver spears, and others were decked out in armour of every colour, all of them clad in iron. With Symeon in their midst, they acclaimed him as emperor in the language of the Romans. All the members of the senate stood on the walls and watched what was happening. One could truly see an imperial and magnanimous soul, and marvel at his undaunted spirit and courageous bearing. Seeing so great an onrush of enemies, he was not dismayed and did not draw back. He went forward with a calm soul, as if he were going to meet a friendly crowd, all but offering himself to the enemy as a ransom for his subjects.
21. So he was the first to arrive at the landing stage and waited there for Symeon. Hostages were taken from both sides, and the Bulgarians searched the landing stage carefully in case there was any trick or ambush. Then Symeon got down from his horse and came in to the emperor. They greeted each other and began to speak of peace. The emperor is said to have spoken to Symeon as follows: "I have heard that you are a God-fearing man and a true Christian, but I see that your deeds do not agree with your words at all. A God-fearing man and a Christian loves peace and embraces love, since God both is love and is called love. It is the impious and the unbeliever who delight in slaughter and in blood unjustly shed. If, then, you are a true Christian, as we have been assured, put an end at last to these unjust slaughters and to this shedding of innocent blood. You are yourself a Christian, both in fact and in name, so make peace with us Christians. Do not wish to defile Christian hands with the blood of fellow Christians. You too are a man, and you await death, resurrection and judgement. Today you exist, and tomorrow you will crumble into dust. A single fever will extinguish all your arrogance. What account will you give to God, then, when you go there, for these unjust slaughters? With what face will you look upon the fearsome and just Judge? If you do these things out of love of wealth, I will fill you to the full with what you desire. Only hold back your hand. Embrace peace. Love concord, so that you yourself may live a peaceful, bloodless and untroubled life. Then the Christians will at last be free of their calamities and will stop killing Christians, for it is not lawful for them to take up arms against their fellow believers." When he had said this, the emperor fell silent. Symeon was put to shame by his humility and his words, and he agreed to make peace. [?]
22. I will now relate a portent that occurred at that time,

something extraordinary to those who know how to interpret such things. They say that while the emperors were talking, two eagles flew over them, screeched, and met each other. They immediately separated again, and one passed over the City while the other flew off toward Thrace. Those who study such things closely judged this to be a bad omen.
