They said that both men would part without reaching any real agreement about peace. When Symeon reached his camp, he told his magnates about the emperor's intelligence and humility. He praised to the skies his appearance, his strength and his undaunted spirit.
23. On the twenty-fifth of December Romanos crowned his sons Stephen and Constantine in the Great Church. The patriarch Nicholas also tonsured Romanos's son Theophylact, a eunuch, as a cleric. He ordained him subdeacon and appointed him synkellos, after Theophylact had first passed through the order of [?] in the sanctuary.
24. On the nineteenth of April Romanos honoured John, the mystikos and paradynasteuon, with the ranks of patrician and anthypatos. For this very reason envy was stirred up against him and some people accused him.
25. On the fifteenth of May, in the thirteenth indiction, the patriarch Nicholas departed this life. He had held the patriarchate for thirteen years since his accession, and his body was laid in the monastery of Galakrenai, which he had founded. In the month of August Stephen, the metropolitan of Amaseia, a eunuch, was installed as patriarch.

26. In the month of October John, the mystikos and paradynasteuon, was accused of aiming at the throne. He was said to be acting at the instigation of the patrician Kosmas, logothete of the drome, who was giving John his daughter in marriage. For this reason John was removed from the palace. He was still allowed to come in, however, to serve the emperor and manage affairs with him. The emperor Romanos had a very great affection for him, because John was able to serve him in everything, and he did not want to drive him away completely. But the accusers kept pressing the emperor and clearly proved their charges. The emperor investigated, learned that they were true and was about to arrest John and question him. John found out in advance and fled. He reached the place called Monokastanon and was tonsured a monk. Constantine Boilas, the epi tes trapezes, who was his intimate friend, also fled. He reached Olympos and he too became a monk, since he had shared the mystikos's plans and been party to his secrets. The emperor had the patrician Kosmas flogged in the Horologion of the [?] and replaced him. In place of John the mystikos he appointed Theophanes as paradynasteuon.

27. At that time a terrible earthquake also struck the Thrakesion theme. The earth split open in a great and terrifying chasm, so that many villages and churches were swallowed up.
28. On the twenty-seventh of May, in the fifteenth indiction, Symeon, the ruler of Bulgaria, died. He had appointed as ruler his son Peter, whom he had by his second wife, the sister of George Soursouboules. Symeon also left George as guardian of his children. Michael, his son by his first wife, he had tonsured a monk. John and Benjamin, Peter's brothers, still wore Bulgarian dress.
29. When the surrounding nations, the Croats and the rest, learned of Symeon's death, they wanted to campaign against the Bulgarians. Famine and locusts were pressing the Bulgarian nation hard. They feared an attack by the other nations, but they feared an invasion by the Romans even more. After taking counsel, they campaigned against the Romans and reached Macedonia. Having struck fear into the Romans, as might be expected, they then learned that the emperor was about to campaign against them. Peter and George secretly sent a monk named Kalokyres, an Armenian by birth, bearing a chrysobull. Its contents stated that they welcomed peace with the Romans and were eager to agree to it. More than that, they were also ready, if the Romans wished, to form a marriage alliance.
30. The emperor received this monk most gladly. He at once sent the monk Theodosios Aboukes and Constantine of Rhodes, an imperial cleric, by dromon to Mesembria to discuss peace with the Bulgarians. They arrived, discussed what was needed and set out overland with Stephen the Bulgarian. George Soursouboules followed and caught up with them. When they reached Constantinople they made peace and asked to form a marriage alliance with the emperor. They saw Christopher's daughter Maria and were greatly pleased with her. After first drawing up agreements about the peace they had made, they wrote to Peter to come quickly.
31. Niketas the magistros, the co-father-in-law of the emperor Romanos, was sent to meet Peter and escort him to the City. When Peter the Bulgarian arrived, the emperor Romanos boarded a trireme and came to Blachernae. He met Peter as he arrived to see him and embraced him. After they had talked together as was fitting, they signed the peace agreements and the marriage contracts. The protovestiarios Theophanes acted as mediator in these matters and continually arranged affairs between the Romans and the Bulgarians.
32. On the eighth of the month of October [?] went out
[?] that the Bulgarians too sealed the documents with [?] [margin] [?]

…the patriarch Stephen, together with Theophanes the protovestiarios, Maria the daughter of Christopher and the whole senate, [went] to the church of the most holy Mother of God at the Source. There they blessed Peter and Maria and placed the wedding crowns on their heads, with Theophanes the protovestiarios and George Sursuvul acting as groomsmen. After a splendid and costly banquet, when all the customary wedding rites had been joyfully completed, Theophanes the protovestiarios entered the City with Maria, the daughter of the emperor Christopher. On the [?] day of the wedding the emperor Romanos gave a splendid feast at the landing-stage of the imperial dromon at the Source, which he had decked with silk hangings. There the emperor Romanos dined with Peter the Bulgarian, together with his son-in-law Constantine and his son Christopher. The Bulgarians insisted strongly that Christopher be acclaimed first and Constantine after him. The emperor Romanos gave way to their insistence, and it was done as they asked. 33–34. When everything to do with the wedding had been completed and Maria was about to set out for Bulgaria with her husband Peter, her parents went with her as far as the Hebdomon, together with Theophanes the protovestiarios. They dined there with Peter, and since he was about to depart they embraced their daughter and shed many tears, as one would at the loss of a dearly loved child. Then they kissed their son-in-law, entrusted her into his hands and returned to the palace. Maria, handed over into Bulgarian hands, went off to Bulgaria rejoicing and grieving at once. She grieved because she was parted from her dearest parents, from the imperial household and from the company of her kin, but she rejoiced because she had been joined to an emperor as husband and proclaimed mistress of the Bulgarians. So she departed, taking with her splendid wealth, [?] and countless baggage. 35. At that time envoys also came to the emperor Romanos from Melitene, offering terms of peace in order to make a treaty. Not long afterwards Apochaps, the grandson of Amer and emir of Melitene, and the general Aposalath, a man of great nobility and wealth, came from Melitene. Romanos received them magnificently and with fitting honour, and after they had [concluded?] a peace agreement they returned home. From then on they campaigned alongside the Romans against their fellow Hagarenes, and they even entered the City with the Romans in their triumphs, leading Hagarene captives. This was a marvellous and astonishing sign of the misfortune of the godless Hagarenes. But when Apochaps, a prudent and sensible [?] man, died, the inhabitants of Melitene broke the peace. So [?] campaigned against them [?]

the domestic of the schools John Kourkouas with the themes and the tagmata, and Melias with the Armenians. They made many raids every day, and by continual incursions they took the people captive and plundered them. They reduced Melitene to such straits that they very quickly sacked it and razed it to the ground. They did the same not only to Melitene but also to its neighbouring cities and lands, which were fertile and very rich and yielded many other revenues. The emperor turned this Melitene into a kouratoreia and arranged that many thousands of gold and silver be paid from it every year as tribute. 36. Niketas the magistros, father-in-law of the emperor Christopher, was accused of urging Christopher to turn against his own father and drive him from the throne. So they took him out of the City and tonsured him a monk, banishing him to his own suburban estate. 37. On 18 July, in the 6th indiction, the patriarch Stephen died, after holding office for 2 years and 11 months. On 14 December they brought Tryphon, a monk living in the Opsikion who was known for his piety and holiness, and ordained him patriarch for a fixed term. He was to serve until Theophylaktos, the son of the emperor Romanos, whom they intended to ordain patriarch of Constantinople, came of age. 38. On the twenty-fifth of the same month an unbearable winter set in, so that the ground was frozen for 120 days. A great famine followed, worse than any that had ever happened, and from it came such heavy mortality that the living could not carry out the dead. When the emperor Romanos saw how unspeakably harsh it was, he made provision worthy of his compassionate and merciful nature and relieved the want caused by the famine with many alms. He closed off the porticoes of the colonnades with doors and boards, so that the snow and cold would not get in on the poor sheltering there. At that time he also built the so-called arklai in all the colonnades, and ordered that silver be given every month to the poor lying in them. He also established the monthly trimisia in the churches, twelve thousand in coined silver. That compassionate soul did not stop at these measures in caring for the poor. He also ordered that three poor men should eat with him every day, and each of them received one nomisma. On Wednesdays and Fridays three poor monks ate with him, and each received the prescribed nomisma. He also followed the custom of the monasteries of having a reading during the meal, and so made the table a double one for himself and his guests,

so that the body was fed with ordinary food while the soul delighted in the fitting pleasure of the words. He listened to them attentively, and they pierced his soul with compunction and drew from him many fountains of tears. 39. Who could describe the faith he had in all monks, and above all in those famed for holiness and piety? For he never saw a monk devoted to virtue without confessing his deeds to him with many tears. Being most faithful and most orthodox, he adorned and brightened all the churches of the City with translucent veils and brilliant lighting. He also never failed to send yearly stipends to the monks in the mountains, on Olympus, at [?] Petra and on the mountain of [?]. He cared and provided for them, summoning to himself those renowned for the active and the contemplative life and gathering the blessings of their prayers. Nor was that all. He also never failed to supply the yearly stipends he had established to those who had shut themselves away for God's sake in the poorest of cells, and to all the monasteries. We have recounted these few out of the many of his countless good deeds and acts of charity. 40. Peter the Bulgarian's brother John, together with other magnates of Symeon, plotted against him. When they were found out, John was beaten and shut up in prison, and the rest were subjected to punishments of no ordinary kind. When Peter reported this to the emperor Romanos, the emperor sent the monk John, who had been rhaiktor. The pretext was to arrange an exchange of the prisoners being held, but in truth he was to secure John and bring him to Constantinople. He boarded a ship with John at Mesembria and came to the City. Not long afterwards John cast off the monastic habit and sought a wife. The emperor gave him a house, a great many estates and a wife who came from the emperor's own homeland, the Armeniakon. He held a splendid wedding at the house of the Caesar, with the emperor Christopher and the monk John, the former rhaiktor, acting as groomsmen. 41. On 2 March a cornice fell in the Forum from the top of the columns standing in a row there and killed 6 men. There was also a great and terrible fire in the colonnade of the Forum near the church of the most holy Mother of God, which burned down the candle shops and the fur shops of the Forum as far as the Psicha. 42. The emperor Christopher died in the month of August, in the 4th indiction. His father mourned him greatly

because he himself had already reached old age and Christopher's sons were still infants. His remains were laid in his father's monastery mentioned above. 43. In the month of August, in the 3rd indiction, they also deposed the patriarch Tryphon, since he had completed the fixed term. He went off to his own monastery and died there. The Church was left widowed for one year and 5 months because Theophylaktos, the son of the emperor Romanos, was still under age, for, as has been said, the emperor intended to install him as patriarch. 44. A certain Basil, an impostor from Macedonia, claimed to be Constantine Doukas and drew many people after him. He was seized by Elephantinos, a tourmarch of the Opsikion, brought to Constantinople, and had one of his hands cut off by the eparch. Later, when he saw his chance, he went back to the Opsikion. He fitted a bronze hand in place of the one that had been cut off, made himself an enormous sword, and again went about deceiving many vagabonds into believing that he was Constantine, the son of Doukas. He drew them along with him and stirred up a great revolt against Romania. He seized a fortress called Plateia Petra and stored every kind of provision in it, and from there he sallied out to plunder and ravage whoever he came across. The emperor sent an army against him, which captured him and those with him. They brought him to the City, questioned him and gave him many blows to make him name his fellow rebels, if there were any. He falsely accused many officials of being his accomplices. But he was proved to have said nothing true against them, and at the Amastrianon he [was given] as fodder to the flames [?]

45. Theophylaktos, the emperor's son who has often been mentioned, was ordained patriarch on 2 February, in the 6th indiction. Legates had come from Rome bringing a synodal tome that authorized his ordination, and they installed him on the patriarchal throne. 46. Maria, the granddaughter of the emperor Romanos mentioned earlier and the wife of Peter, emperor of Bulgaria, came to the City to visit her father and her grandfather. The last time she came, she brought three children, and her father Christopher had already died. She received great and valuable riches from her grandfather and returned home with honour. 47. The emperor Romanos took a wife for his son Stephen. She was the daughter of Gabrielios and the granddaughter of Katakylas, and her name was Anna. Together with the wedding crown, the crown of empire too [was placed on] him [?]

…and they overran the land as far as the City and took captive every soul in Thrace. So the patrikios Theophanes, the protovestiarios and chief minister, was sent to arrange an exchange with them. He dealt with them admirably and shrewdly and achieved everything he wanted, and they praised and admired him greatly for his prudence and sound judgement. On that occasion the emperor Romanos also displayed his generosity and humanity, sparing no expense to ransom the captives. 49. The emperor Romanos took a wife for his youngest son Constantine from a family of the Armeniakon. Her name was Helena, and she was the daughter of the patrikios Adrian. When she died in the month of February, in the 2nd indiction, he married Constantine to another. 50. On 11 June, in the 15th indiction, the Rus' sailed against Constantinople with ten thousand ships. The patrikios Theophanes, chief minister and protovestiarios, was sent against them with whatever triremes and dromons happened to be in the City. He prepared and readied the fleet in advance, fortified himself as best he could with fasting and tears, and waited for the Rus', intending to fight them at sea. When they arrived and came near the Pharos, he was lying in wait at the mouth of the Euxine Sea, at the place called Hieron, and he suddenly attacked them. He sailed through first in his own dromon, broke up the formation of the Rus' ships, burned a great many of them with the prepared fire and put the rest to flight. The other dromons and triremes followed him out and completed the rout. They sank many ships with all hands, wounded many men and captured a great many alive. The survivors sailed over to the eastern shore, to the place called Sgora. Bardas Phokas was then sent by land with picked horsemen to shadow them. When the Rus' sent a sizable detachment into Bithynia to obtain food and other supplies, Bardas Phokas came upon it and dealt harshly with them, routing and slaughtering them. At that time John Kourkouas, magistros and domestic of the schools, also came down with the whole army of the East. He destroyed many of them, catching stragglers here and there, so that they shrank back for fear of his attack, stayed together by their ships and dared not range anywhere. 51. Before the Roman army came down, they had committed many terrible crimes. They burned the whole of the area called the Stenon, and of the captives they took, some they crucified,

others they nailed to the ground, and others they set up as targets and shot with arrows. As for the members of the priestly clergy they captured, they tied their hands behind their backs and drove iron nails into the middle of their heads. They also set fire to many holy churches. With winter now setting in and food running short, and fearing both the army that had arrived and the triremes fighting them at sea, they decided to make for home. They were eager to slip past the fleet, and in the month of September, in the 15th indiction, [they tried] to sail across [?] … [but Theophanes showed?] a most watchful and noble spirit. A second sea battle was joined at once, and that man sank a great many ships and killed many of them. A few escaped with their ships, ran onto the shore of Koile and fled as night came on. The patrikios Theophanes returned with a brilliant victory and the greatest of trophies. He was received with honour and magnificence and was given the rank of parakoimomenos. 52. John Kourkouas the magistros mentioned above proved an outstanding soldier. He set up many great trophies, extended the Roman frontiers and sacked a great many cities of the Hagarenes. Because the man's valour was so conspicuous, the emperor Romanos wanted to take John's daughter as a bride for his grandson Romanos, the son of his son Constantine. But this plan stirred up envy against him among the other emperors, and he fell from office. The patrikios Pantherios, a relative of the emperor Romanos, was appointed domestic in his place. 53. In the 1st indiction, in the month of April, the Turks attacked again with a very large force. The patrikios Theophanes the parakoimomenos went out and made a peace treaty with them, taking hostages from among their notables. As a result the peace was kept for 5 years. 54. In the second indiction the emperor Romanos sent Paschalios, protospatharios and strategos of Longobardia, to Hugh, king of Francia, to ask for his daughter as a bride for Romanos, the son of his son-in-law Constantine. Paschalios received her and brought her to the City with great wealth. The wedding took place in the month of September, in the 3rd indiction. She lived for 5 years and died during the sole reign of her father-in-law Constantine. 55. In the month of December a very violent wind blew, and the so-called demes in the Hippodrome

collapsed. These were the ones that stood opposite the imperial box, and they smashed the benches beneath them and the so-called stethea. When the year had come round, in the same month, his sons brought the emperor Romanos down from the palace. 56. The city of Edessa, where the precious imprint of Christ was kept, was being besieged by the Roman army and reduced to the direst need. Its inhabitants sent envoys to the emperor Romanos asking that the siege be lifted and promising to hand over the holy imprint of Christ. In return for this favour they asked to receive [?] prisoners from among their notables and to be given chrysobulls guaranteeing that their land would no longer be plundered by the Roman army. This was done. The holy imprint was sent off, and when it was already nearing Constantinople, the patrikios and parakoimomenos Theophanes went out to the river Sangarios and met it with lamps, fitting honour and hymns. On 15 August they entered the City with it, while the emperor [waited?] at Blachernae and venerated it there. On the next day the emperor's two sons, Stephen and Constantine, and his son-in-law Constantine went out to the Golden Gate with the patriarch Theophylaktos. They received it with fitting honour and carried it on foot to the holy church of the Holy Wisdom of God, with the whole senate going before it and a great procession of lights leading the way. They venerated it there and then brought it up to the palace. 57. In those days a prodigy from Armenia visited the City. It was a pair of [twin?] boys joined together, born from a single womb. They were sound and complete in every limb of the body, but they were joined from the pit of the stomach down to the lower belly, facing each other. They stayed in the City for a long time and everyone looked on them as an extraordinary prodigy, but in the end they were driven out of the City as an evil omen. They came back during the sole reign of Constantine. When one of them died, some skilled physicians cleverly cut through the part where they were joined in the hope that the other would live, but he survived for three days and then died. 58. As was said above, the emperor Romanos had boundless faith in all monks. He especially honoured and revered Sergios, who shone among the monks. Sergios was the brother of the magistros Kosmas and the nephew of the patriarch Photios, but his nobility of soul brought him more honour than his distinguished family. He reached the summit of both virtue and learning, so that it was hard to tell in which he excelled more, so far had he carried each of them. Besides his other qualities, he also had the gift of discernment, a gracious

character and a modest mind. He did not raise his eyebrows as the wise men of today do, and he never seemed boastful or arrogant. His speech dripped sweeter than honey, his character was firm and steady, and his mind was humble. The emperor kept this celebrated man with him constantly, a true rule and measure that always set his life straight. He often urged the emperor to take care of his sons and not to leave them undisciplined and inclined to wickedness, lest he suffer the fate of Eli and pay the penalty for his sons' lawlessness. 59. When his sons brought him down from the palace and exiled him to the island of Prote, he again had this man as a consolation in his misfortunes and a soothing remedy for his sorrows. Also with him at that time was Polyeuktos, a most pious monk, who likewise offered him fitting consolation. On the death of the patriarch Theophylaktos, Polyeuktos was appointed patriarch of Constantinople under the emperor Constantine. 60. God wills to save man in many ways, and so he allowed the emperor Romanos to fall into an unexpected misfortune, so that, chastened by it and brought to recognize his own sins, he might be found worthy of salvation. For he allowed his son Stephen to rise up against him, just as Absalom once rose up against his own father David. Stephen took as his advisers in this the former monk Marianos, Basil Peteinakes the protospatharios and Manuel Kourtikes, and the other emperors were also in on the plot. He wickedly brought his father down from the palace, exiled him to the island of Prote and had him tonsured a monk. 61. So Constantine, Romanos' son-in-law, was left as sole ruler. He at once honoured Bardas, the son of Phokas, with the rank of magistros and appointed him domestic of the schools, since he had long shown his valour in war. Next he made Basil, surnamed Peteinakes, patrikios and great hetaireiarch. He stripped Marianos, of the family of the Argyroi, of the monastic habit and made him patrikios and count of the stable, and likewise he made Manuel, called Kourtikes, patrikios and droungarios of the watch. Not long afterwards God's just judgement overtook these three, for they had raged against the Lord's anointed and laid hands on him unjustly, coveting the empire. Each of them was caught in treason and ended his life by a most pitiful death. We shall set out the fuller and more detailed account of them in the main narrative [?]. 62. Forty days later, on 27 January, Constantine began to suspect that the emperor Stephen and his brother Constantine would do the same to him. He reasoned, naturally enough, that if they had not [spared?] their own father

…[?] how they would spare him. Having given them a feast, [?] while they sat at table, with the food still in their mouths, they were seized by the men called the Hornikioi, the patrician Marianos, and the others who had been made ready for this. They took them down from the palace, confined them on the nearby islands, and tonsured them as clerics. 3. A little later they asked to see their own father, and came to him on the island of Prote. When they saw him in the monastic habit, they were overcome by unbearable grief. Their father wept over them and said: “I begot sons and raised them up, but they have rejected me.” After that they were sent into exile: Stephen to Proconnesus, from Proconnesus to Rhodes, and from Rhodes to Mytilene; Constantine to Tenedos, and from there to Samothrace, where he plotted a revolt and was killed by the men guarding him. As for Michael, the son of Christopher, the emperor stripped him of the imperial sandals and made him a cleric. 4. While the emperor Romanos was on the island, the patriarch Theophylact and the patrician and parakoimomenos Theophanes laid a plan to bring him back to the palace. They shared it with him and won him over, and then watched for the right moment to carry the plan through. But when the plot was discovered and reported to the emperor Constantine, he punished those who had taken part in it: he exiled the patrician Theophanes, and he had the protospatharios and pinkernes George and the primikerios Thomas flogged, tonsured, and paraded through the middle of the city, and then sent them into exile. 5. In the month of December of the sixth indiction, some men plotted against the emperor Constantine, intending to bring the emperor Stephen from the island back to the palace. [p. 594] When this plot was reported to Constantine by Michael, known as Diabolinos, the emperor seized the conspirators. Some he had their noses and ears cut off; others he subjected to an unbearable flogging. He set them on donkeys, paraded them through the middle of the city, and sent them into exile. 6. On the fifteenth of the month of July, in the sixth indiction, the emperor Romanos died on the island of Prote. His body was brought to the city and laid to rest in his own monastery.
